 On the morning of October 17th, at the opening session of the 2nd Session of the 16th National Assembly, Prime Minister Le Minh Hung presented a report on the implementation of the socio- economic development plan for 2026 and key tasks and solutions for the remaining months of the year.
 According to the Prime Minister , the international and regional situation continues to be very complex, with many new issues arising beyond expectations. Strategic competition is becoming increasingly fierce, conflicts are disrupting global supply chains, while policy adjustments by countries are strongly impacting economic growth and international trade, increasing inflationary pressure, especially on gasoline prices and many strategic commodities.
 In this context, the Government and the Prime Minister have closely followed the resolutions and conclusions of the Party and the National Assembly to concretize them into action programs and plans; at the same time, they have innovated working methods, organized implementation, and proactively handled unexpected and emerging issues.
 Government revenue is projected to exceed 3 trillion VND.
 According to the report, the socio-economic situation has achieved many important results, with 14 out of 15 key indicators expected to meet or exceed the set targets.
 Regarding economic growth, the Prime Minister stated that GDP in the third quarter increased by 9.95%, bringing the growth rate for the first nine months to 9.01%, placing it among the highest in the region and the world . Notably, economic growth maintained a trend of higher growth in each subsequent quarter.
 Along with promoting growth, the government is focusing on stabilizing the macroeconomy, controlling inflation, and ensuring the major balances of the economy.
 Fiscal, monetary, and other macroeconomic policies were managed proactively and flexibly. State budget revenue for the whole year is estimated at 3.06 trillion VND , an increase of 14%, while the total amount of tax and fee exemptions, reductions, and extensions is approximately 360,000 billion VND .
 By the end of 2026, public debt is projected to be at 33-34% of GDP, government debt at approximately 32-33% of GDP, and national foreign debt at around 28-29% of GDP. The budget deficit is expected to be around 4.1% of GDP, within safe limits.
 Regarding monetary matters, the Prime Minister stated that the exchange rate remains stable and the liquidity of the credit system has improved.
 Notably, the State Bank of Vietnam has implemented measures to manage and direct the system of credit institutions to uniformly reduce lending interest rates by 1.5-2% for production and business activities and priority sectors, in accordance with the policies of the Central Government and the Prime Minister.
 The Vietnamese stock market also received its first-ever upgrade. Along with this, Moody's raised Vietnam's outlook from stable to positive. According to the report, international organizations highly appreciate the resilience and growth prospects of the Vietnamese economy. 
|  | 
|  The Prime Minister reports to the National Assembly on the implementation of socio-economic targets. Photo: Quochoi.vn. | 
 Regarding price management, the Prime Minister stated that in the context of sharply rising crude oil prices and many other commodities, the Government has implemented a comprehensive set of measures to boost domestic petroleum production, diversify import sources, and promptly utilize tax, fee, and state budget tools.
 As a result, the supply of petroleum products is ensured, and fuel prices remain low compared to the region.
 In the electricity sector, the rational mobilization and regulation of power sources has helped ensure supply and prevent electricity price increases amidst unprecedentedly high demand, especially to serve growth targets, investment in science and technology, and the development of data centers.
 Price management and control efforts continued to be implemented, contributing to keeping the average consumer price index (CPI) increase for the first nine months at 4.52%.
 Besides macroeconomic stability, all three economic sectors recorded relatively strong growth, and the economic structure continued to shift positively.
 In the first nine months, the industrial and construction sector grew by 11%, the highest rate since 2015. Agriculture remained stable, while the service sector developed positively. The number of international visitors to Vietnam reached 17.7 million, an increase of 15%, the highest ever.
 Notably, the Prime Minister also stated that import and export activities had increased by more than 30% after nine months, forecasting that the total import and export turnover for the whole year would reach an estimated $1.11 trillion , exceeding the trillion-dollar mark for the first time.
 Regarding investment, total social investment capital in the first nine months is estimated at 3.11 million billion VND , an increase of 15%. Public investment disbursement reached nearly 643,000 billion VND , equivalent to 63% of the plan, almost 13% higher than the same period last year.
 Registered foreign direct investment reached US$50.36 billion , a 76% increase, the highest since 2021. The capital flow was concentrated in the processing, manufacturing, high-tech, electronics, and semiconductor sectors.
 Continue to lower interest rates.
 Regarding institutional reform, the Prime Minister stated that the Government has been submitting to the National Assembly many important laws and resolutions with mechanisms and policies aimed at removing bottlenecks, unlocking resources, and supporting production and business.
 The focus will be on policies to exempt or reduce taxes, raise tax thresholds, and create superior mechanisms to mobilize resources for growth regions and poles.
 The government is also focusing on shifting from support to robust business development, especially for private enterprises; unlocking land resources, developing social housing and rental housing, and addressing long-standing issues, particularly projects in the land, energy, and healthcare sectors.
 At the same time, the Government is consolidating four national target programs, increasing autonomy for localities, and reviewing and improving mechanisms and policies to significantly reduce input costs.
 These include drastic measures to reduce real estate prices, minimize intermediaries, and contribute to boosting production and business activities, improving efficiency and competitiveness of the economy.
 Regarding administrative procedure reform, the Government focused on addressing overlapping and inadequate regulations, and overcoming delays in issuing and backlog of guiding documents. According to the report, the time taken to process administrative procedures was reduced by 53%, and compliance costs for citizens and businesses decreased by 55%, the largest reduction ever.
 Referring to the key tasks in the remaining months of 2026, the Prime Minister emphasized the need to strive to achieve the highest possible results for the set targets and indicators, especially the double-digit growth target, while maintaining macroeconomic stability and controlling inflation.
 First and foremost, the government is focusing on effectively managing fiscal, monetary, and other macroeconomic policies, while simultaneously implementing decisive and effective measures to further reduce lending interest rates.
 This also includes ensuring the supply of electricity and fuel; promoting the domestic market through demand-stimulating measures, effectively exploiting the year-end consumption and tourism season, while controlling and stabilizing prices.
 The Prime Minister also called for boosting exports and reducing the trade deficit.
 For localities, the head of government urged them to strive vigorously to achieve the highest possible growth rates, especially in major growth poles.
 Another key task is to strive for 100% disbursement of public investment plans, while simultaneously promoting private investment, attracting foreign investment, and resolving outstanding projects.

articles.summary: Choose the right breakthrough areas and improve implementation efficiency to achieve double-digit growth.  Vietnam.vn

| Chairman of the Economic and Financial Committee Phan Van Mai presents the verification report - Photo: Duc Thanh. | 
 With a target of 10% or more growth in the 2027 plan, the Economic and Financial Committee emphasized that the decisive issue is not adding more solutions, but rather choosing the right breakthrough areas, improving implementation efficiency, productivity, and the self-reliance of the economy.
 The room for further monetary policy easing is increasingly limited.
 On the morning of October 17th, presenting a summary of the review of the implementation of the socio-economic development plan for 2026 and the projected plan for 2027 at the opening session of the second National Assembly session, the Chairman of the Economic and Finance Committee, Phan Van Mai, stated that, despite many difficulties and challenges, the socio-economic situation in 2026 continued to achieve important and fairly comprehensive results in many areas. It is projected that 9 out of 15 key indicators will meet or exceed the plan, 5 indicators will strive to meet, and 1 indicator on multidimensional poverty reduction is not expected to be achieved.
 The auditing agency also noted several key issues that need attention in future guidance and management.
 That is, high growth but an unstable foundation. The four localities with the largest economies (Ho Chi Minh City, Hanoi , Hai Phong, and Dong Nai), accounting for nearly 47% of total GRDP, are all projected to fall short of their 2026 growth targets. Private investment has not truly broken through, accounting for 53% of total social investment but only increasing by 14%, the lowest among the three sectors. Exports increased by 24.5% but imports increased by 36.7%, resulting in a trade deficit of US$19.42 billion; exports are heavily dependent on the FDI sector, while supporting industries, localization rates, and technological mastery remain limited. Labor productivity improvement is slow. Growth in scale has not been accompanied by improvements in productivity, domestic added value, and the self-reliance of the economy.
 The next point raised by Mr. Mai was the increasing pressure to stabilize the macroeconomic situation and ensure financial safety. The average CPI for the first nine months increased by 4.52%, already at the target of approximately 4.5% for the whole year, with a 4.80% increase in the third quarter alone; prices of essential goods and services are rising, while actual purchasing power is recovering slowly.
 Credit growth is outpacing deposit mobilization, resulting in a high credit-to-GDP ratio; the capital market has not adequately met medium- and long-term needs, placing a heavy burden of capital supply on the banking system, increasing the risk of maturity mismatches and liquidity pressure; risks between banks, corporate bonds, and real estate are interconnected and easily amplified. The room for further monetary policy easing is increasingly limited, Mr. Mai noted.
 The audit report also highlighted the numerous difficulties faced by businesses and household businesses. In the first nine months, the number of businesses entering and re-entering the market decreased by 3.2%, while the number of businesses completing dissolution procedures increased by 118.8%. Small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) struggle to access capital and face pressure from input costs, logistics, and compliance costs. Household businesses face a slow recovery in purchasing power while simultaneously adapting to digital transformation , governance, and tax policy requirements. These difficulties directly impact investment, employment, income, and domestic demand.
 Maintaining macroeconomic stability is a prerequisite for high growth.
 Regarding the projected socio-economic development plan for 2027, the Review Committee basically agreed with the orientation, objectives, targets, and 11 groups of tasks and solutions proposed by the Government .
 “The target of GDP growth of 10% or more reflects strong determination but poses a significant challenge given the unstable growth foundation, inflationary pressures, and increasing demand for capital and energy. Some opinions suggest clarifying the growth scenario and developing solutions for each sector, locality, and new growth drivers; closely assessing the growth potential of major economic centers, the room to control CPI at around 4.5%; and the consistency and feasibility of major balances,” Mr. Mai reflected.
 While acknowledging that the Government's 2027 task and solution framework basically covers immediate requirements and medium- and long-term orientations, the reviewing agency suggested that the plan for the following year should focus on a few key areas to overcome the problem of being too scattered and to clarify priorities.
 First, we must steadfastly maintain macroeconomic stability, considering it a prerequisite for high growth; placing the coordination of fiscal, monetary, and price management policies at the center. We must leverage the proactive role of fiscal policy with a focus on key areas, cautiously utilizing monetary leeway, and determining safe thresholds for each instrument; controlling credit quality, non-performing loans, and liquidity; and developing capital markets to reduce dependence on the banking system.
 This also involves innovating the growth model towards in-depth development and increasing domestic added value. It requires unlocking, allocating, and utilizing resources from public investment, private investment, state-owned enterprises, FDI, and the financial market in a coordinated and efficient manner. The focus should be on solutions to support the development of small and medium-sized enterprises and business households, especially in accessing capital, reducing input costs, logistics costs, and compliance costs; creating conditions for domestic enterprises to participate in supply chains; and ensuring that solutions are feasible, utilize resources efficiently, and meet the practical needs of businesses.
 The review committee also recommended focusing on developing foundational and supporting industries; attracting selective FDI linked to technology transfer, developing domestic suppliers, and increasing the localization rate. Simultaneously, it suggested strengthening domestic demand; controlling trade fraud; expanding exports, leveraging FTAs, and proactively responding to trade barriers and green standards. It also urged the prompt completion of mechanisms and policies to bring the international financial centers in Ho Chi Minh City and Da Nang into effective operation, contributing to attracting international capital flows.
 “The Economic and Financial Committee emphasizes that implementation is the decisive factor. It proposes clearly defining responsibilities, deadlines, resources, and expected outcomes for each task; strengthening inspection and supervision; and linking implementation results to the accountability of the head of each agency. The overarching requirement is to link high growth with macroeconomic stability, sustainable development, and a substantial improvement in the material and spiritual lives of the people,” Chairman Phan Van Mai reported to the National Assembly.

 Proactive management and maintaining growth momentum.
 In 2026, Ninh Binh's economy will be affected by many unfavorable factors. Fluctuations in tariff policies, competition among major countries, and rising fuel and transportation costs will impact production and exports. Within the province, the need to complete planning, develop infrastructure, and improve the efficiency of local government operations at both levels requires sectors and localities to address immediate issues while preparing for the next phase of development.
 Following the directives of the Central Government, the leadership of the Provincial Party Committee, and the resolutions of the Provincial People's Council, the Provincial People's Committee has proactively concretized the goals and tasks for 2026; updated the growth scenario, and identified sectors and fields that need focused promotion. Management has been implemented in a way that is closely connected to the grassroots, linking task assignments with progress reviews and accountability of heads of departments. Provincial leaders have focused on on-site inspections and direct meetings with businesses, concentrating on issues that significantly impact development: land, land clearance, investment procedures, budget revenue, and the progress of key projects. The Provincial People's Committee regularly maintains the "Government Accompanying - Businesses Developing" program, linked with addressing specific requests and creating conditions to maintain production and implement projects.
 Simultaneously, the province is actively implementing policies to develop the private economy, improve the efficiency of the state-owned economy, develop science and technology, and promote digital transformation . Planning, investment attraction, urban development, and infrastructure development continue to receive attention, gradually exploiting the advantages within the province's development space.
 Under the direction and management of the Provincial People's Committee, the involvement of all levels and sectors, and the efforts of the business community, the economy maintained a fairly strong growth momentum in the first nine months. Industry continued to be the main driving force, with the industrial production index estimated to increase by 25.01% compared to the same period last year; the processing and manufacturing sector increased by 25.38%. Production of laptops, trucks, and electrical products showed significant growth, helping to offset the difficulties faced by some other manufacturing sectors.
 Trade, services, and exports continued to grow. Total retail sales of goods and consumer service revenue were estimated at VND 239,674 billion, an increase of 20.9%; export turnover reached USD 28,132 million, an increase of 50%. These results demonstrate the adaptability of businesses and affirm the role of consumption and exports in the local economy.
 Tourism was a bright spot, exceeding the annual plan in both visitor numbers and revenue. The province is estimated to have welcomed 20.96 million visitors, an increase of 25.5%, exceeding the plan by 4.79%; revenue is estimated at 21,979 billion VND, an increase of 23.5%, exceeding the plan by 9.89%. Promoting heritage values, expanding linkages, diversifying products, and improving service quality have contributed to boosting trade and service activities, creating jobs and income for the people.
 Basic agricultural production remained stable, with a comprehensive bumper crop of the spring season. Production linkage models, emission-reducing farming practices, and technology applications continued to expand.
 Investment activities continued to supplement resources for the economy. Total implemented investment capital in the province reached VND 125,188 billion, an increase of 5%; non-state capital increased by 12.7%, and FDI capital increased by 16.2%. In the first nine months, the province granted licenses for 124 new projects and adjusted capital increases for 80 projects. The results of attracting investment, along with the development of businesses, create further conditions for expanding production and enhancing competitiveness in the coming years.
 Overcome limitations, determined to achieve the goal.
 Despite the achievements, the province's economy still faces challenges that need to be addressed. Some businesses producing automobiles, glass, and fertilizers are under pressure from market conditions, raw materials, and costs. Production of passenger cars (under 10 seats) decreased by 10.9% compared to the same period last year. The number of businesses temporarily ceasing operations or dissolving remains high, indicating that the resilience of some businesses is still limited.
 Notably, land use fee collection and public investment disbursement have not met expectations. According to the Provincial People's Committee's report on the review of its leadership and management, as of September 28th, total budget revenue in the province reached approximately 46,657 billion VND, equivalent to 58.13% of the provincial People's Council's projected target; land use fee collection only reached 27.24% of the projected target. Capital from the 2026 public investment plan disbursed was approximately 12,710 billion VND, equivalent to 36.1% of the plan assigned by the Prime Minister . These limitations directly affect the ability to balance resources and the progress of infrastructure development.
 Land clearance for some projects is still slow; difficulties in resettlement, land ownership verification, and land-use conversion have not been addressed promptly. Material supplies are sometimes insufficient, and price increases have led to project adjustments and construction delays. The Provincial People's Committee report also frankly points out that the responsibility of leaders is unclear in some areas, inter-agency coordination is slow, and inspections and monitoring are not frequent enough. The operation of the two-tiered local government system still faces obstacles regarding decentralization, coordination procedures, and implementation capacity at the commune level. These limitations need to be overcome so that the policies and solutions issued can be effective in practice.
 Firmly committed to achieving a GRDP growth rate of 11% or higher in 2026, the Provincial People's Committee requested a review of all targets based on the results of the first nine months, classifying those likely to be exceeded, met, or at risk of not being met. For those at risk of not meeting the target, specific solutions, roadmaps, and responsibilities must be identified in the fourth quarter, and growth scenarios must be closely monitored for timely management. The focus is on continuing to remove obstacles for businesses, ensuring conditions for electricity, water, infrastructure, and land for production; promoting projects that can create additional production capacity, jobs, and revenue. Activities supporting access to capital, technological innovation, digital transformation, and market expansion must be closely aligned with the needs of businesses. Trade and tourism should continue to build on achievements, improve service quality, and effectively exploit the province's potential and advantages.
 Regarding public investment, the province focuses on land acquisition for key projects, reviewing the progress of each project, and evaluating disbursement results in conjunction with accountability. Accelerating progress must go hand in hand with project quality, investment efficiency, control of advances, and prevention of loss and waste. Projects that are unlikely to disburse funds need to be reviewed, processed, or have their capital reallocated according to regulations. Revenue collection is linked to the implementation of the land fund development plan, streamlining procedures for each project, and urging the fulfillment of identified financial obligations.
 Simultaneously, strengthen the management of revenue from production and business, combat revenue losses, and nurture revenue sources; manage expenditures according to actual balance capabilities, prioritizing investment in development and social welfare. The year-end tasks are also placed within the requirements for preparing the 2027 plan and the 2026-2030 period. Completing the planning, developing connecting infrastructure, addressing outstanding projects, and improving the quality of governance and human resources will create conditions for achieving the goal of building Ninh Binh into a centrally-governed city before 2030, characterized as a Millennium Heritage City and a creative city.
 Therefore, achieving the 2026 target is crucial for fulfilling the tasks of the entire term. This determination needs to be demonstrated through the responsibility of each agency and locality, and through the progress and results of each task. Substantive changes in production, investment, resource management, and services to the people and businesses will strengthen the foundation for Ninh Binh to maintain high, sustainable growth and move towards long-term goals.

JAKARTA – Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto replaced disaster management chief Suharyanto on Oct 15, a day after Suharyanto’s younger brother was arrested over alleged corruption involving emergency relief funds.
The leadership change comes as Indonesia battles widespread forest and peatland fires in Sumatra and Kalimantan, with haze spreading to neighbouring Singapore and Malaysia.
Lieutenant-General Kristomei Sianturi, 50, was appointed to replace Suharyanto, 59, as head of the National Disaster Mitigation Agency (BNPB). This was announced at the Presidential Palace in Jakarta, alongside nine other appointments, including those of Yusuf Jauhari and Richard Tampubolon as deputy defence ministers, and forestry professor Satyawan Pudyatmoko as head of the National Peatland and Mangrove Management Agency (BPGMN).
Kristomei, a two-star army general, previously commanded troops in the Sumatran provinces of Lampung and Bengkulu and served as a spokesman for the Indonesian military and army. Suharyanto, a former senior army officer, has led BNPB since November 2021 following his appointment by then President Joko Widodo. There is no fixed tenure for the agency’s chief, and no official reason was given for his replacement.
Speaking to reporters after his appointment, Kristomei pledged to act swiftly to tackle the forest fires and review the agency’s operations. “The target is as soon as possible. We must not allow people to continue suffering the consequences,” he said. “We are counting minutes, not hours.”
Wasisto Raharjo Jati, a political analyst at the National Research and Innovation Agency, said the change aims to restore public confidence amid regional scrutiny of Indonesia’s handling of the fires.
“The failure to fully resolve the forest fires, which have affected Malaysia and Singapore, has damaged the government’s image within ASEAN, particularly after Malaysia sought to raise the issue at a regional forum. This reshuffle is certainly part of efforts to restore the government’s image domestically and internationally,” he told The Straits Times.

Malaysian Foreign Minister Mohamad Hasan said on Oct 12 that he would raise the transboundary haze issue at an ASEAN foreign ministers’ meeting in Manila in November.
Wasisto said the arrest of corruption suspects at BNPB was another factor behind the leadership change. Indonesia’s anti-graft agency had arrested five people, including Bima Setyawan, the younger brother of BNPB chief Surhayanto, over alleged corruption involving emergency relief funds, as forest fires blanket parts of South-east Asia in haze and put pressure on the country’s disaster response efforts.
The Corruption Eradication Commission (KPK) detained the suspects on Oct 14, a day after carrying out raids in Jakarta and surrounding areas, over suspected irregularities in the procurement of goods and services at BNPB.
KPK chairman Setyo Budiyanto said investigators were examining indications of collusion between agency officials and private companies over the disbursement and use of emergency funds. “There are indications of arrangements being made, particularly over the disbursement and use of funds, some of which were misused by certain individuals for personal gain,” he told reporters on Oct 14.
The investigation centres on BNPB’s ready-to-use emergency funds, known locally as dana siap pakai, which are used to meet urgent needs during disasters, including buying essential supplies and services.
The agency was allocated about 4.62 trillion rupiah (S$330 million) in such funds for 2026, according to The Jakarta Post. KPK has not said whether any money earmarked for tackling the ongoing forest fires was involved.
Emergency procurement rules allow agencies to appoint suppliers directly because of the urgency of disaster response, but Setyo stressed that such spending remained subject to regulations.
Bima serves as an expert staff member to his brother Suharyanto. The other suspects are Gabriel Purwaka Sigit, a BNPB official in charge of procurement commitments; Richard Erlangga, another expert staff member; and two private-sector representatives, Gery Prasetiawan and Syifa Nrika Ghifarian. Setyo said Suharyanto was not named as a suspect.
Asked about the corruption investigation, Kristomei said BNPB would not interfere with the legal process and that officials could be replaced if necessary. “We will leave the matter entirely to law enforcement authorities to investigate. There will be no interference from BNPB,” he said.
However, Setyo stressed that investigators would focus on individual responsibility, regardless of family connections, adding: “What matters here is that the individual who committed or is suspected of committing an unlawful act is the one being held accountable.”
KPK’s investigators seized about 3.3 billion rupiah in cash, as well as hundreds of grams of gold and cryptocurrency, during the operation, in which 14 people were initially taken in for questioning.
It is investigating suspected conflicts of interest in procurement and other alleged corruption offences, including claims that an official used his position to approach private suppliers and arrange procurement activities. “By being in that position, he took advantage of his status and then approached several parties whom I would describe as vendors or service providers,” Setyo said, without naming the suspect.
Setyo said the suspected irregularities may have stretched back three or four years. “Perhaps from 2022 until now, 2026, or perhaps 2023, I have forgotten,” he said.
KPK has yet to establish the total amount allegedly misappropriated, how much may have been diverted for personal gain, or the precise goods and services involved in the procurement.
The government has deployed about 70,000 personnel from BNPB, the military, police and other agencies to contain the blazes.
The claims have prompted lawmakers to demand greater scrutiny of disaster relief spending.
Indonesian MP Abdullah, also known as Abduh, called for a comprehensive audit of BNPB’s finances by the country’s State Audit Board. “If funds that should have been used to help disaster victims were instead misappropriated, we must ask how many people may have been deprived of the assistance they needed,” he said.
KPK has not ruled out widening the investigation if further evidence emerges or other individuals are implicated.
BNPB acting spokesman Berton Panjaitan said the agency respected the legal process and would cooperate with investigators. He acknowledged some disruption to its work, but said public services and disaster response operations would continue despite the arrests.
Indonesian MP Abdul Wachid expressed dismay at the alleged corruption, particularly as the country grapples with disasters. “It is deeply troubling. At a time when the country is being hit by disasters and people are suffering, how can anyone exploit the situation for corruption?” he said.

articles.title: America’s $40 Trillion Debt Problem: Who Will Ultimately Pay the Price? - CEOWORLD magazine
articles.summary: America’s $40 Trillion Debt Problem: Who Will Ultimately Pay the Price?  CEOWORLD magazine
articles.full_text:
The United States can borrow in its own currency, giving it extraordinary financial flexibility. But that advantage cannot eliminate the economic cost of federal debt. Inflation, higher interest rates, currency depreciation, political dysfunction, and pressure on retirement benefits reveal how the burden can spread across investors, businesses, taxpayers, and households.
The United States occupies a privileged position in global finance. Its government borrows overwhelmingly in dollars, the currency at the center of international banking, trade, and foreign exchange reserves. Its Treasury securities underpin financial markets, while the Federal Reserve possesses monetary capabilities unavailable to governments dependent on foreign-currency borrowing.
Yet America’s monetary advantages have limits. The federal government may be able to meet its dollar-denominated obligations without preserving the purchasing power of every dollar it repays. Even when Treasury investors receive their principal and interest on schedule, inflation, exchange-rate movements, and rising financing costs can redistribute the economic burden.
For corporate executives and institutional investors, understanding these mechanisms is essential. Fiscal deterioration can influence capital allocation, financing conditions, retirement security, and global investment flows long before a conventional sovereign debt crisis develops.
1. Debt Ceiling Confrontations Can Undermine Treasury Market Confidence
The United States faces an unusual institutional risk: Congress can authorize spending while separately limiting the Treasury’s borrowing capacity.
This contradiction has repeatedly produced confrontations over the federal debt ceiling.
In 1979, operational problems and complications surrounding the borrowing limit contributed to delayed payments on approximately $120 million in Treasury bills. The obligations were eventually settled, but the episode demonstrated that even American government securities were vulnerable to administrative and political disruption.
The 2023 debt ceiling confrontation again exposed investors to uncertainty over whether particular Treasury obligations might be paid late.
Such episodes matter because Treasury securities serve as benchmarks for financing throughout the global economy.
Even a temporary disruption can damage confidence, increase the compensation demanded by creditors, and complicate financial-market operations.
The principal danger is institutional. A government capable of meeting its obligations can nevertheless create payment uncertainty through political disagreement.
2. Governments Can Change the Monetary Terms of Their Obligations
American history offers an extraordinary example of how sovereign debt commitments can be altered during a financial emergency.
Before the Great Depression, certain government obligations contained gold clauses intended to protect creditors against changes in the dollar’s monetary value.
In 1933, Congress invalidated gold-payment provisions in public and private contracts. The following year, the official gold price increased from approximately $20.67 to $35 per ounce, reducing the dollar’s gold value by roughly 41%.
Creditors could receive the promised nominal dollars without receiving the originally contemplated gold equivalent.
In 1935, the Supreme Court ruled that Congress had exceeded its authority in repudiating the government’s gold obligations, but the bondholder before it did not obtain additional monetary recovery.
The episode illustrated the difference between contractual promises, sovereign monetary authority, and enforceable financial remedies.
Modern Treasury securities operate within a different legal and monetary system. Nevertheless, proposals to extend maturities or negotiate special arrangements with creditors raise related questions.
Any coercive restructuring of American debt would carry potentially substantial legal, diplomatic, and reputational costs.
The United States benefits from investor confidence in the reliability of Treasury obligations. Undermining that confidence could outweigh the immediate savings from changing repayment terms.
3. Dollar Depreciation Can Transfer Losses to Foreign Investors
The dollar’s international role gives Washington substantial borrowing flexibility, but foreign investors remain exposed to changes in its exchange rate.
Under the postwar Bretton Woods system, eligible foreign monetary authorities could exchange dollars for gold at an official price of $35 per ounce.
That arrangement became increasingly difficult to sustain as dollar liabilities expanded relative to American gold reserves.
In August 1971, the United States suspended dollar convertibility into gold, helping bring the Bretton Woods monetary framework to an end.
The resulting international monetary system left foreign holders of dollar-denominated assets increasingly exposed to market-determined currency movements.
Consider a European pension fund holding US Treasury bonds.
The Treasury can meet every contractual obligation, yet the fund may experience a loss measured in euros if the dollar depreciates sufficiently.
Currency depreciation is not sovereign default. Nevertheless, it can reduce the foreign-currency value of American financial obligations.
There is an important constraint.
Foreign governments, central banks, and institutional investors hold dollar assets partly because of the depth, liquidity, and institutional infrastructure of American financial markets.
If confidence in the dollar’s long-term purchasing power deteriorates, investors may demand higher yields, increase hedging, or diversify reserves.
America’s reserve-currency advantage therefore depends on preserving the credibility that makes dollar assets attractive.
4. Inflation Can Reduce Debt While Eroding Household Wealth
Inflation can reduce the real value of outstanding fixed-rate government debt.
The mechanism is straightforward. When prices increase, a dollar repaid in the future purchases fewer goods and services than a dollar borrowed today.
The United States experienced this dynamic after the Second World War.
Wartime borrowing had expanded federal debt substantially. In the following decades, economic growth, inflation, and interest-rate arrangements contributed to a significant decline in debt relative to national output.
During part of this period, government financing benefited from policies that held nominal interest rates below prevailing inflation.
This combination is associated with financial repression, in which financial regulations or monetary arrangements help maintain government borrowing costs below market-clearing levels.
The consequences extend beyond Treasury investors.
Households holding low-yield savings, pension funds with fixed-income investments, and insurers managing long-term liabilities can experience purchasing-power losses.
However, inflation is an imperfect fiscal instrument.
As existing Treasury securities mature, the government must refinance obligations at prevailing interest rates. Investors expecting sustained inflation generally demand higher nominal yields.
Inflation may therefore reduce the real burden of older debt while increasing the cost of newly issued securities.
The Federal Reserve’s credibility becomes particularly important. Political pressure to suppress interest rates despite persistent inflation could damage confidence in monetary stability.
For executives, the resulting uncertainty complicates wage negotiations, investment appraisal, long-term contracting, and financing decisions.
5. Higher Treasury Yields Spread Fiscal Pressure Across the Economy
America can continue servicing its obligations while paying progressively more to borrow.
This outcome avoids default but creates another form of economic adjustment.
Treasury yields influence financing conditions across mortgages, corporate bonds, commercial real estate, bank lending, and leveraged acquisitions.
When government borrowing costs increase, private-sector financing frequently becomes more expensive.
For households, higher mortgage rates reduce purchasing power and housing affordability.
For corporations, they can weaken the economics of capital investment, acquisitions, and debt-funded expansion.
Private equity firms and heavily leveraged businesses face particular sensitivity when existing debt must be refinanced.
The federal government experiences similar pressure.
As lower-coupon Treasury securities mature, refinancing them at higher yields increases interest expenditures. Unless offset by higher revenues or lower spending, those costs can widen deficits and increase future borrowing requirements.
The source of rising yields matters.
An increase driven by stronger productivity and economic growth can accompany improving corporate earnings.
An increase driven by persistent inflation, deteriorating fiscal expectations, or a larger term premium presents a different investment environment.
Institutional investors should distinguish these drivers rather than treating every increase in Treasury yields as evidence of fiscal distress.
6. Retirement Benefits Could Become Part of the Fiscal Adjustment
Federal debt sustainability also intersects with the government’s long-term spending commitments.
Social Security illustrates the distinction between contractual government borrowing and statutory benefit programs.
Treasury securities are debt obligations. Social Security benefits arise under legislation that Congress can amend.
The retirement system depends primarily on payroll-tax revenue and accumulated trust fund reserves. Demographic changes have increased the pressure on its financing arrangements.
Official projections indicate that dedicated reserves will become insufficient to support scheduled benefits in the coming years unless legislation changes the system’s finances.

The 2026 Annual Meetings of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank Group began on October 12, 2026, at the Queen Sirikit National Convention Center in Bangkok and are due to close officially on October 18.
Global financial and fiscal leaders have held intensive discussions on a range of major economic issues throughout the past week.
Bangkokbiznews has compiled 22 key takeaways from the discussions and presentations at the meetings.
The IMF launched its latest annual flagship report, “Shaping the Future of Asia: Opportunities and Challenges”, examining the region’s economic growth and achievements over several decades.
Since 1990, Asian economies have accounted for almost two-thirds of global economic growth.
Their contribution has been particularly strong in 2026, reaching a record 68% of worldwide growth.
The IMF launched its World Economic Outlook, entitled “Resilience Under Strain, Urgent Choices”, with a clear policy message to governments and central banks worldwide that fiscal policy needs to tighten.
Governments need to act quickly to reduce budget deficits and contain public debt, end blanket cash handouts and restrict cost-of-living subsidies to vulnerable groups within clearly defined timeframes.
On monetary policy, central banks need to maintain their independence and hold interest rates at sufficiently restrictive levels to prevent rising prices from spiralling out of control over the long term.
Although global growth remains uneven, the IMF noted that Thailand, as a member of the ASEAN-5 group of economies within the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), benefits indirectly through technology supply chains.
Investment in artificial intelligence (AI) hardware infrastructure by leading Asian producers such as South Korea and Taiwan has provided some support for Thai manufacturing and exports.
AI has become an important contributor to global trade and economic growth.
Between 2023 and 2025, world trade expanded by a cumulative 8.3%, while trade in AI-related goods rose by 29%.
Excluding those goods, global trade growth would have been just 4.6%.
The World Bank argued that reducing poverty requires a focus on creating opportunities through work, beyond providing financial assistance.
With government budgets and aid resources under pressure, it is adjusting its strategy to bring in greater support from philanthropy and the private sector.
Support through official development assistance (ODA) currently amounts to one-fifth, or US$15–20 billion annually, alongside efforts to mobilise private capital.
The private sector is the main engine of global job creation, accounting for 90%.
Developing countries do not always need the largest or most advanced AI technologies, according to the World Bank.
Under its “Small AI” approach, the emphasis is on adapting technology to local circumstances to deliver productivity gains and economic growth.
The approach addresses infrastructure constraints associated with large language models (LLMs) in developing countries by focusing on practical applications.
Examples include remote screening for skin diseases in Indonesia and using photographs to analyse crop diseases in India.
The climate crisis is raising costs and increasing the vulnerability of Thai businesses, particularly through flood damage and pressure to adapt quickly to a low-carbon economy.
Access to finance and insurance remains a key challenge in building business resilience.
The World Bank proposed integrating policies for micro, small and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs) with green finance and insurance mechanisms to improve disaster preparedness and maintain competitiveness.
This is particularly relevant to small businesses in flood-prone areas with limited resources to adapt.
The World Bank highlighted structural changes in global trade over the past 30–40 years.
Trade has quadrupled, while developing countries’ share has doubled.
Half of developing countries’ trade is now conducted with one another, reflecting a shift from earlier patterns of dependence on developed export markets.
The figure given for ASEAN’s trade within the region was 50–55%, reflecting stronger regional trading ties than those in South Asia, Africa or Latin America.
Although 100 bilateral and multilateral trade agreements have been signed worldwide over the past decade, inadequate implementation remains a major problem.
The World Bank therefore called for faster action to reduce trade barriers.
The World Bank highlighted that 1.2 billion young people in emerging economies will reach working age in the coming years.
With adequate support for healthcare, the environment and education, they could become a significant force for economic growth.
MSMEs account for 75% of employment in developing countries.
The World Bank has launched a new strategy to help these businesses obtain finance, improve competitiveness and create sustainable local jobs, particularly in low-income or conflict-affected countries.
Despite successive shocks from the pandemic, wars and energy prices, the global economy has proved more resilient than expected.
This partly reflects the private sector’s flexibility and rapid adjustment, alongside policy buffers accumulated by emerging market economies.
The World Bank argued that Thailand and ASEAN need to accelerate regional economic integration, remove non-tariff trade barriers and strengthen supply chains and digital infrastructure links.
Building on existing regional trading ties would improve resilience and create opportunities as global trade becomes increasingly fragmented.
MSMEs form a foundation of developing economies, accounting for 90% of businesses and 75% of employment, according to the World Bank.
Over the next 10–15 years, 1.2 billion people in developing countries will reach working age, while their economies are expected to create only 420 million jobs.
To address these constraints, the World Bank proposed four strategies using data and digital technology to support MSMEs.
These involve making businesses visible within the system, connecting them with markets and services, reducing barriers to doing business and widening access to finance.
Budget constraints and high public debt present another major challenge for developing countries.
Successive global crises over the past decade, from COVID-19 to wars and tensions in the Middle East, have left many governments with less fiscal space.
The World Bank noted that governments must decide how to allocate resources between infrastructure essential for economic development, particularly AI-related infrastructure, and investment in human capital, such as education.
Both are important for long-term growth.
The World Bank is working with Japan’s government, the World Health Organization (WHO) and global partners to advance universal health coverage (UHC) through “country compacts”.
These allow countries to define their own needs while drawing targeted financial support from partners such as Gavi and the Global Fund.
A UHC Knowledge Hub has also been established to bring finance and health ministries together for a full year to plan reforms that make health financing more efficient and self-reliant.
With public debt rising worldwide, the IMF warned that governments in advanced economies could return to policies that helped reduce debt after the Second World War.
Known as “financial repression”, these use financial policies and regulations to keep government borrowing costs below market levels, with savers bearing the burden indirectly.
Rather than relying on announced tax increases or explicit austerity measures, this approach operates through the financial system.
Regulations encourage, or pressure, banks and financial institutions to hold more government bonds than market conditions would otherwise justify.
Governments obtain cheaper funding, while people receive lower returns on their deposits and investments.

The IMF argued that countries should go beyond adopting AI and promote its use throughout the economy and among all population groups so that the economic benefits are widely shared.
Developing human capital is crucial for ASEAN.
The highest priorities were described as covering four areas, with workforce upskilling, refocusing the education system and lifelong learning listed.
AI is reshaping jobs rather than eliminating them.
Although demand for workers in roles that AI can replace initially fell by 10%, that decline has begun to stabilise.
Demand for workers equipped to work with AI, meanwhile, is clearly increasing, suggesting a change in working practices rather than the wholesale replacement of labour.
The IMF described AI as a technology spreading at unprecedented speed, offering significant growth opportunities to countries connected to its value chain.
However, only a minority of countries have access to those opportunities, while financial stability risks are becoming an issue for policymakers to monitor.
The world remains at an early stage of the transition.
Most visible gains involve improvements in individual efficiency rather than economy-wide productivity.
The discussion referred to “Amara’s Law”, which holds that people tend to overestimate the short-term impact of new technology and underestimate its long-term effects.

Deputy Prime Minister Nguyen Van Thang has requested the State Bank of Vietnam (SBV) to urgently implement measures to reduce lending interest rates by 1.5 to 2 percentage points for production, business activities, and priority sectors to support citizens and enterprises.
The directive was issued during a meeting on monetary policy management for the final months of the year, held on October 16.
Assessments shared at the meeting indicated that prevailing lending interest rates remain elevated, adversely affecting capital costs and restricting access to credit for both businesses and individuals. Meanwhile, global economic developments continue to exert upward pressure on interest rates, exchange rates, and inflation.
The Deputy PM urged the central bank to execute timely, substantive measures to bring down overall interest rate levels, specifically targeting a 1.5–2% cut in loan rates for production, commerce, and priority sectors. The Governor of the SBV is directly tasked with overseeing these efforts, bearing responsibility for implementation outcomes while ensuring adequate liquidity across commercial banks.
Credit institutions must trim operating costs, enhance operational efficiency, lower lending rates, and publicly disclose interest rate schedules in full compliance with regulations. The SBV was instructed to step up inspections, audits, and strictly penalize any financial institutions failing to comply with rate-cut directives or engaging in unfair interest rate competition.
In addition, Mr. Thang called for directing credit flows into production, commerce, and priority sectors, alongside the continued rollout of government-mandated credit support programs.
Regarding the social housing loan program, the central bank was asked to provide refinancing at reasonable interest rates to participating commercial banks.
The Deputy PM also ordered strict oversight of credit quality and decisive resolution of non-performing loans (NPLs), especially bad debts linked to real estate. Authorities must accelerate the restructuring of weak credit institutions and eliminate cross-ownership, hidden ownership, and manipulation within the banking sector.

articles.title: Moving Manufacturing From China to Mexico - Harris Sliwoski LLP
articles.summary: Moving Manufacturing From China to Mexico  Harris Sliwoski LLP
articles.full_text:
When China's COVID-zero lockdowns and its aggression toward Taiwan started spooking foreign companies in 2022, the international manufacturing lawyers at my firm began getting a steady stream of calls and emails from companies looking to leave China. Most wanted to know about Mexico, and some of the companies calling us were themselves Chinese or Taiwanese. The tariff wars since then have given companies more reasons to look south. Mexico makes sense for many of them. But companies that go into Mexico expecting to find China with a shorter shipping route are in for an expensive education.
Starting in 2022, my good friend Andrew Hupert and I wrote a long series of posts for this blog on what leaving China for Mexico actually involves. Nobody was better suited to write about this than Andrew. I first met him in Shanghai in 2003, and over the following two decades I came to rely deeply on his practical business wisdom, especially about China. When my firm stepped up its China practice, he was one of my go-to people on all things China. He was a business school professor who taught negotiation around the world, and he spent more than 20 years in Asia, living and working in Shanghai, Taipei, Hong Kong, and Saigon. Though he had tied his career to China, he, like me, was an early believer in a post-China manufacturing world. He moved to Thailand and then Vietnam, and when Mexico began emerging as a leading replacement for China manufacturing, he moved to Monterrey and then Oaxaca, and became fluent in Spanish. He spent his last years there helping companies, especially companies leaving China, set up and run operations in Mexico. Few people had spent as much time thinking about how the two countries compared, and fewer still had Andrew's willingness to say exactly what he thought.
Andrew died of a heart attack in Oaxaca in October 2024, at 61. I wrote about him and our friendship in Remembering Andrew Hupert. This guide brings our Mexico work together in one place and updates it for 2026. Most of the business and cultural observations are Andrew's, drawn from his years running and advising operations in both countries. The legal and trade analysis is mine, informed by my firm's affiliated lawyers in Mexico City and the United States, and by many of the conclusions Andrew and I reached together over the years. Andrew is no longer here to update his words, so I have done that as best I can. Where events have proved us right or wrong, I say so. When I quote him, the words are his as he wrote them. I want readers to understand where his observations came from and why I continue to think they matter.
In early 2023, Andrew and I wrote that running a supply chain entirely through China had become a bet against the house, the kind that ends with the gambler up a ton at midnight and borrowing bus fare home by morning. The trade numbers seemed to argue otherwise. U.S.-China trade had hit a record $690 billion in 2022, and plenty of companies took that as vindication of their decision to stay. Multinationals were reading the situation differently. Their supply chain planners, the Lean Production and Six Sigma people who treat unnecessary risk as a sin, were piling into Mexico, as Unilever's $400 million commitment to a new plant in Nuevo León showed that same month. When a Chinese surveillance balloon was shot down over the United States that February, we predicted that cooler heads would not prevail. Washington, we said, would keep changing the economics of China supply chains by every means available, and Beijing would answer each new U.S. restriction with its own. We saw little reason to expect either government to put the interests of companies caught in the middle ahead of its own political priorities.
We put governments at the top of the list of likely supply chain shocks and said the damage would most likely come through mistakes, meaning bad regulations written and enforced for non-economic goals. Would governments knowingly hurt their own economies for a good soundbite? "Yes. Of course they would. We expected U.S. customs to demand ever more detailed proof that your goods were not made with forced labor in Xinjiang. Complying would trap your China staff in a catch-22, because trying to trace the origin of your materials could get them "invited to tea" by the authorities. We also expected Beijing to retaliate, since, as we put it, "Beijing will not apologize; it will reply." China has a long record of using trade to punish countries that anger it, including Japan, Norway, Canada, South Korea, Australia, and Lithuania. And we warned that after the disruptions of 2021 and 2022, no owner or fiduciary could credibly claim a China supply chain disruption was impossible to foresee. Many of our clients already had China exit and evacuation plans, and we told readers they should too. That advice was based on what we were already seeing companies struggle with, long before the current tariff battles. See Doing Business with China and Your Reputation Risks and Repeat After Me: Trade Relations Between the United States and China Will Only Get Worse.
Tariffs and trade restrictions have since vindicated much of what we wrote. In 2023, Mexico overtook China as the top source of U.S. goods imports, at $475.6 billion to China's $427.2 billion, with China's total down 20 percent from 2022. Real U.S. imports from China fell 28 percent in 2025 alone, and by year-end the average U.S. tariff on Chinese goods was near 50 percent, up from 21 percent when the second Trump administration took office. Beijing retaliated most effectively with rare earth export controls. It suspended its expanded October 2025 controls for one year, until November 10, 2026, but its April 2025 controls on seven medium and heavy rare earths remain in force. The forced-labor scrutiny we predicted has also become a basis for tariffs. In July 2026, the U.S. Trade Representative imposed tariffs on goods from 60 economies, China and Mexico among them, after finding that they had failed to impose and effectively enforce bans on imports made with forced labor. Our biggest mistake was assuming North American trade would remain politically protected. We underestimated just how willing Washington would be to make life difficult for companies manufacturing in Mexico, a subject I discuss below.
Companies that left China early told us their decisions had paid off. In that same 2023 series, Andrew and I passed along what clients who had moved their manufacturing elsewhere were saying. One said he slept better, both because he worried less about his supply chain and because he felt better about no longer supporting such a brutal regime. Another had left before COVID, which let it avoid the China tariffs, underprice its competitors, and take a good chunk of market share while those competitors scrambled to catch up. Others said they were hiring people who chose them because they had nothing to do with China. Still others had customers choosing them because their products did not come from China, whether to reduce supply chain risk or reputational risk. These were business owners explaining what had happened to their companies, and their experiences were far more persuasive than another consultant's presentation about geopolitical risk. We also said the most unforgivable sin foreign companies committed in China was going there without an exit strategy. I still believe that, and I would build an exit strategy into any Mexico plan from the start as well.
One of the most important differences between manufacturing in China and Mexico is how much control you have over the risks your business faces. Every country has problems. Factories lose power, employees leave, suppliers fail, and shipments get delayed. You can reduce many of these risks by investigating your suppliers, choosing your location carefully, and making sure you have alternative sources of supply. You can never eliminate every manufacturing risk, but there is a great deal you can do to keep ordinary business problems from becoming disasters.
Many of Mexico's biggest manufacturing risks fall into that category. Security is a serious concern, but you can investigate specific locations and arrange safer transportation. Labor laws are demanding, but you can hire Mexican employment lawyers and structure your operation to comply with them. Infrastructure varies considerably, but you can check whether a proposed site has reliable power and water before committing to it. None of these precautions guarantees that your operation will run smoothly. They do, however, give you meaningful ways to reduce your exposure.
China presents some risks that no amount of good management can bring under your control. You can investigate your suppliers and trace your materials, but you cannot eliminate the possibility that U.S. Customs will detain your goods over forced-labor concerns. You cannot prevent Beijing from imposing export restrictions or Washington from raising tariffs. You can prepare for a crisis involving Taiwan, but you cannot prevent one. A company can do everything right inside its Chinese factory and still find its business badly damaged by a political decision made thousands of miles away. That is what makes these risks especially troubling. The company has very little ability to influence the decisions that create them.
Mexico has political risks of its own, as the 2026 USMCA review and the latest tariffs demonstrate. A Mexican manufacturer cannot control what Washington decides about North American trade any more than a Chinese manufacturer can control U.S. policy toward China. I would never suggest otherwise. But when comparing countries, I would pay particular attention to which risks you can realistically manage and which ones can overwhelm your business regardless of how carefully you operate. That distinction is one of the strongest reasons many companies have decided they would rather manufacture in Mexico.

articles.title: Vietnam, Switzerland to turn education, sci-tech, innovation into cooperation focus - Vietnam+ (VietnamPlus)
articles.summary: Vietnam, Switzerland to turn education, sci-tech, innovation into cooperation focus  Vietnam+ (VietnamPlus)
articles.full_text:
Hanoi (VNA) – Prime Minister Le Minh Hung and Swiss President Guy Parmelin agreed to turn education – training, science – technology, and innovation into the focus of the two countries’ cooperation during their meeting in Hanoi on October 17. 
Warmly welcoming the Swiss President on his official visit to Vietnam, which coincides with the 55th anniversary of the two countries’ diplomatic relations, PM Hung affirmed that Vietnam always deeply values the precious support and assistance provided by the Swiss Government and people throughout its past struggle for national independence and reunification, as well as its ongoing development and international integration. 
Vietnam consistently regards Switzerland as a reliable friend and an important partner in Europe, he stressed, expressing his wish to further enhance political trust, increase high-level mutual visits and engagements, optimise existing cooperation mechanisms, and establish an intergovernmental cooperation framework in the economy, science – technology, and innovation at an early date. 
He noted that the visit opens a new chapter in bilateral relations, particularly marked by the signing of the free trade agreement between Vietnam and the European Free Trade Association (VEFTA). 
Highly appreciating Switzerland's active role in promoting the signing of the agreement, the Government leader called for joint efforts to ensure VEFTA takes effect promptly, thus driving breakthroughs in trade and investment cooperation and doubling bilateral trade turnover in the near future. 
He also encouraged Swiss businesses and investment funds to expand their presence in Vietnam across fields such as finance – banking, manufacturing, biotechnology, pharmaceuticals, and innovation. 
Highlighting finance as Switzerland’s paramount strength and a strategic development orientation for Vietnam, PM Hung called on Switzerland to share its expertise, support the development of an international financial centre in Vietnam, and facilitate the centre’s linkages with major global financial hubs. 
He further proposed strengthening cooperation in green finance, investment funds, asset management, crypto assets, carbon credits, international bonds, and financial technology. 
Expressing his pleasure at visiting Vietnam again, President Parmelin emphasised that his country was among the first to establish diplomatic ties with Vietnam, adding Vietnam’s image in Switzerland continues to grow increasingly positive. 
The Swiss leader held that the two countries share many similarities, particularly in upholding peace, cooperation, and multilateralism. 
Switzerland attaches importance to its relationship with Vietnam and seeks to promote substantive and effective cooperation, he stated, noting that the presence of numerous Swiss businesses and scientists in his delegation reflects strong interest in and high expectations for the potential of bilateral cooperation. 
He expressed his delight at the signing of VEFTA, which will open up vast opportunities to boost the two countries’ trade, investment, and business connectivity, especially for small and medium-sized enterprises. 
Confirming Switzerland’s readiness to share its experience and expertise in insurance, reinsurance, manufacturing, precision machinery, and high technology, the President proposed connecting Switzerland’s Crypto Valley with Vietnam’s innovation ecosystem, and advancing ties in blockchain, artificial intelligence (AI), and quantum technology. 
He specifically highlighted vocational training collaboration tailored to business needs, and affirmed the readiness to further facilitate visa issuance for Vietnamese citizens. 
At the meeting, the two sides agreed to continue strengthening the Vietnam–Switzerland Comprehensive Partnership across Party, State, parliamentary, and people-to-people channels. 
They pledged to effectively utilise VEFTA, boost business connectivity, and expand investment links, including in seaport infrastructure. They also agreed to coordinate in reinforcing the multilateral trading system, diversifying markets, and enhancing resilience against global economic fluctuations. 
The two leaders concurred in making education – training, science – technology, and innovation the focus of bilateral cooperation. They pledged to promote ties between innovation hubs, research institutes, universities, and enterprises, while stepping up collaboration in AI, quantum technology, green energy, the digital economy, higher education, and vocational training. 
Addressing common challenges posed by climate change, both sides agreed to step up cooperation in emissions reduction, green transition, agronomic research, water resource management and reuse, sustainable agricultural development, as well as insurance and reinsurance. 
They were also unanimous in fostering links in culture, tourism, labour, and people-to-people exchanges. 
Vietnam and Switzerland reaffirmed their commitment to maintaining close coordination and mutual support at multilateral forums, thereby helping reinforce the Comprehensive Partnership and actively contributing to peace, stability, cooperation, and development regionally and globally./.
