articles.full_text:
Deputy Prime Minister and Finance Minister Ekniti Nitithanprapas has positioned Thailand as a leader ready to help steer 191 countries through turbulent global economic waters alongside the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank Group.
Drawing on the image of the Royal Barge Suphannahong, Ekniti compared Thailand’s role to that of the figure at the front who sets the direction as the crew rows in unison through rough water. He argued that countries needed the same sense of purpose to confront economic uncertainty together.
“Thailand would like to show ourselves as a trusted connector, so we can connect everyone—191 countries together—to be on the same boat for one week,” he said, emphasising the importance of sharing ideas, responsibilities and a common goal of improving people’s lives.
Ekniti outlined the vision on Saturday (October 17) as Thailand unveiled the Bangkok Dialogue Notes, a collection of reflections from the 2026 IMF–World Bank Group Annual Meetings, taking place at the Queen Sirikit National Convention Center from October 12 to 18.
More than 19,000 people had registered, the highest total in the event’s history, according to the host country’s statement. Ekniti identified three achievements: international recognition for Thailand’s hosting capabilities, a role in shaping the global economic agenda and a stronger position as a trusted connector.
He warned that geopolitical and geoeconomic fragmentation, artificial intelligence (AI), higher energy prices and living costs, rising borrowing costs and climate disruption were testing economies worldwide. Technological advances and international investment could create new opportunities, but their benefits were becoming increasingly uneven, particularly for smaller businesses and vulnerable communities.
“True resilience comes not from isolation, but from trusted connections that help societies withstand challenges and create opportunities for people,” Ekniti emphasised.
The Bangkok Dialogue Notes are not negotiated international agreements or formal policy recommendations. Instead, they draw together reflections from exchanges among policymakers, international institutions, businesses and thought leaders, with an emphasis on turning discussions into practical cooperation.
Five key themes underpin the Bangkok Dialogue Notes:
“If you cannot build trust locally, you cannot connect globally,” Ekniti stressed, warning that investment would encounter resistance if local communities were excluded from its benefits.
Thailand’s Host Country Programme identifies four strategic priorities for translating these principles into action:
“Attracting capital investment is good, but you have to turn capital into capabilities,” Ekniti argued, emphasising the need to equip Thai workers and businesses with the skills and resources to participate in global supply chains.
As an example of practical regional cooperation, Ekniti highlighted plans to advance the ASEAN Power Grid. Hydropower from Laos could be transmitted through Thailand and Malaysia to Singapore, potentially extending to Indonesia, under a multi-year approach that would continue across successive ASEAN chairmanships.
He also urged ASEAN members to establish shared targets for regional trade, investment and digital integration, noting that intra-regional trade accounted for only about 22% of the bloc’s total.
On economic policy, Ekniti urged governments to respond to higher energy costs with targeted support for vulnerable groups rather than broad subsidies, while maintaining fiscal discipline.
He attributed Thailand’s relatively modest rise in government bond yields to fiscal discipline and early fiscal consolidation, arguing that these measures had strengthened market confidence amid rising borrowing costs internationally.
At home, he outlined three goals agreed with the private sector: raising Thailand’s potential economic growth rate to more than 3%, increasing investment from around 22% to 30% of gross domestic product, and securing a place among the top 20 in an international competitiveness index.
The finance minister also described efforts to strengthen ties with European counterparts, explore Islamic finance partnerships and sustain dialogue with global investors through the World Economic Forum’s “Road from Bangkok to Davos” initiative.
The host country’s programme took global discussions beyond conference rooms through dialogues, thematic pavilions, youth activities and exhibitions highlighting Thai communities. The Royal Pavilion presented the development principles and Sufficiency Economy Philosophy of the late King Bhumibol Adulyadej the Great.
Ekniti singled out IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva’s reference to the late King’s teachings at the plenary session as a particularly meaningful moment, linking the principle of patient, people-centred development to the week’s discussions.
He argued that the value of Thailand’s international engagement would ultimately depend on stronger local economies, with investment in human capital, digital systems and energy infrastructure needed to prepare the country for future growth.
“At the end of the day, no matter what we do, we must go back to the people, go back to local communities, understand them and empower them to become resilient and ready for Thailand’s next phase of growth.”

articles.title: To move forward, we need to create more value in the economy. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: To move forward, we need to create more value in the economy.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
(DTTC) - Vietnam has entered the upper-middle-income group. This is a new milestone, not a destination. The challenge is to create more value from every dollar of capital, every hectare of land, and every hour of labor.
For many years, Vietnam's development has been driven by increased investment, expansion of agricultural land, the shift of labor from agriculture to industry, attracting foreign direct investment (FDI), and adopting technology from abroad.
This approach was suitable for the early stages of industrialization. But conditions are different now. Wages are rising. The population is aging faster. Industrial land, energy, and infrastructure are all becoming more expensive. Export markets are imposing stricter requirements on technology, the environment, and product origin. The economy must create more value from its existing resources.
Vietnam has many advantages, but every advantage has its limits. If productivity, technology, and management capacity are not upgraded accordingly, the growth momentum will slow down. The expansionist mindset is quite evident in how many localities attract investment. The number of industrial parks, the area of land converted, registered capital, and the number of new projects are often considered outstanding results.
However, after 5 or 10 years, specific questions need to be answered: How much added value does 1 hectare of industrial land generate? How many Vietnamese businesses become suppliers? How many high-paying technical jobs are created? What are the energy consumption and environmental costs?
Exports have been a major success for Vietnam. In the first nine months of 2026, export turnover reached over US$434 billion, an increase of 24.5%. Processed industrial goods accounted for 90.4% of the total turnover. However, considering economic sectors, the FDI sector generated US$350 billion, accounting for 80.7% of total export turnover. The domestic economic sector accounted for only 19.3%. During the same period, domestic enterprises had a trade deficit of over US$34 billion, while the FDI sector had a trade surplus of nearly US$15 billion.
These figures show that Vietnam has enormous production and export capacity, but the role of domestic businesses is limited. A product exported from Vietnam may have high value, but the revenue retained will be small if the components, design, technology, and brand are all held by foreign companies.
Investment incentives should be linked to post-licensing outcomes: the number of domestic suppliers employed, the number of Vietnamese engineers trained, research and development activities conducted in Vietnam, and the level of technology transfer. These commitments need to be quantified and periodically reviewed.
The way resources are allocated must also change. Capital must find its way to areas of productivity and prospect. Financial markets cannot allocate too much of their resources to real estate and speculation, while innovative businesses lack long-term capital. Land, energy, data, and business opportunities must be accessible transparently.
According to the Provincial Competitiveness Index (PCI) survey for 2025, published by the Vietnam Federation of Commerce and Industry , 75.5% of businesses are unable to obtain loans without sufficient collateral.
If credit mechanisms rely too heavily on collateral, research, technology, and business model innovation will struggle to secure long-term funding. Therefore, there is a need to develop more lending models based on cash flow and business plans.
From 2026 onwards, growth reports need to include specific indicators: How much value do Vietnamese businesses retain from exports? How much income does 1 hectare of industrial land generate? How many domestic businesses become high-level suppliers? What proportion of long-term capital is allocated to technology? Do productivity and wages of workers increase together?
Professor Tran Tho Dat
Stock markets, corporate bonds, and venture capital funds must become efficient capital channels. The state can share some of the risk during the research, testing, and commercialization phases of technology. When a project enters the market, competitive discipline must be ensured.
People are the foundation of productivity. Universities and vocational training institutions need to align their training programs with the actual needs of businesses. Businesses must also allocate resources for on-the-job training. In an era of rapidly changing technology, workers' knowledge needs to be updated throughout their employment.
You may also like
Businesses need stable policies, predictable procedures, and reasonable compliance costs. For small businesses, a steady order or the opportunity to become a supplier to a large corporation is often more practical than general support programs.
Entering the upper-middle income group is a significant milestone. From this point on, the measure of success must be more specific: the ability to create and retain more value within the Vietnamese economy.
* Mr. DANG VIET BACH,Vice President of the Vietnam Young Entrepreneurs Association:
Forming a large business ecosystem
Mr. Dang Viet Bach
Double-digit growth cannot simply be the sum of the growth rates of individual provinces and cities, but must be the result of interconnectedness. This interconnectedness allows raw material sources in the Northwest to reach seaports at lower costs; enables small businesses in Phu Tho, Hung Yen, or Bac Ninh to participate in global supply chains; allows data from one locality to create value for the entire region; and transforms the advantages of each locality into shared advantages for the whole region.
It is necessary to strengthen linkages between leading enterprises, between large and small and medium-sized enterprises, and between enterprises within each industry and value chain, in order to form a broad, efficient, and substantive business ecosystem.
When operating within such an ecosystem, Vietnamese businesses are not only well-equipped to cope with market fluctuations but also collectively drive double-digit growth nationwide, in a rapid and sustainable manner.
* Mr. BUI XUAN BINH,Chairman and CEO of GG Power:
Mastering technology and the value chain.
Mr. Bui Xuan Binh
To realize Vietnam's aspiration of becoming a developed, high-income country by 2045, the economy cannot continue to rely solely on capital, resources, or the advantage of cheap processing and assembly. High and sustainable growth requires a fundamental shift from participating in to mastering the value chain.
Vietnamese businesses need to boldly invest in research and development (R&D), mastering advanced technologies, instead of just focusing on assembly. In addition, strengthening linkages between the government, research institutions, and the business community is necessary to build a robust domestic ecosystem, improve labor productivity, and reduce compliance costs.
You may also like
From the business perspective, we must proactively innovate in management, raise product standards, accelerate automation and digitalization, and quickly expand into the global market (Go Global) to test our competitiveness.
* Ms. NGUYEN THI HOA,General Director of Viettel International Investment Joint Stock Company:
Reaching out internationally, expanding growth potential.
Ms. Nguyen Thi Hoa
To contribute to Vietnam's aspiration of becoming a high-income country, Vietnamese businesses need to boldly expand into international markets and assert their competitiveness. Businesses need to cultivate a global mindset, remain steadfast in product quality, maintain strict implementation discipline, and demonstrate resilience and tenacity in the face of external challenges.
We hope the government will implement more strategic action programs like Go Global, along with mechanisms for protection, support, and economic diplomacy, creating a launching pad for Vietnamese businesses to confidently invest and operate in the global market.

articles.full_text:
On the afternoon of October 17th, under the chairmanship of National Assembly Chairman Tran Thanh Man and the direction of National Assembly Vice Chairwoman Nguyen Thi Hong, the National Assembly heard Minister of Finance Ngo Van Tuan and Chairman of the Economic and Finance Committee Phan Van Mai present reports and verification reports on the implementation of the state budget in 2026, the state budget estimates, the central budget allocation plan for 2027; the implementation of the public investment plan in 2026 and the projected public investment plan for 2027.
We are determined to strive to disburse 100% of the allocated public investment capital.
Reporting on the budget implementation situation in 2026, Minister of Finance Ngo Van Tuan stated that state budget revenue is estimated to reach over 3.05 trillion VND, exceeding the projected figure by 20.8% and increasing by 14% compared to 2025. The ratio of revenue to GDP is approximately 20.8%. Policies to exempt, reduce, and extend tax payments totaling approximately 360 trillion VND have been implemented to support the economy.
Expenditures reached nearly 3.68 million billion VND, equivalent to 116.4% of the budget estimate, ensuring the implementation of the Party's policies, important tasks, debt repayment, aid, etc. Regarding the public investment plan, by the end of September 2026, 62.9% had been disbursed, higher than the same period in previous years both in absolute terms and percentage. The Government is determined to strive to disburse 100% of the allocated public investment capital.
The state budget deficit is estimated at approximately 598.3 trillion VND, about 4.1% of GDP, a decrease of more than 7.5 trillion VND compared to the forecast. It is projected that by the end of 2026, public debt will be around 33 to 34% of GDP, within the limit permitted by the National Assembly.
Overall, Minister Ngo Van Tuan assessed that the management of the state budget and the implementation of fiscal policy in 2026 were proactive, flexible, and timely in supporting businesses and people, and supporting economic growth.
However, some issues also arise, such as: revenue collection progress tends to slow down in the last months of the year, the disbursement of public investment capital still does not meet requirements and deadlines due to obstacles related to procedures, land clearance, rising raw material prices, and implementation organization.
Regarding the state budget estimates, the central budget allocation plan, and the public investment plan for 2027, the Minister of Finance stated that the projected revenue is approximately 3.33 trillion VND, an increase of about 9.1% compared to the estimated actual revenue in 2026. The state budget revenue mobilization rate is approximately 20.2% of GDP, a high target compared to recent years, given the ongoing difficulties and challenges in the world and the region.
The government also submitted to the National Assembly a plan to divide four types of taxes, including corporate income tax, personal income tax, special consumption tax, and environmental protection tax, into four groups of localities to fully implement decentralization in accordance with Central Committee Conclusion No. 18 and the State Budget Law.
Generating resources to achieve double-digit economic growth targets.
You may also like
Regarding the 2027 expenditure budget, the Minister stated that the total state budget expenditure will be approximately 4.07 million billion VND, an increase of 915.2 trillion VND compared to the 2026 budget. Of this, the development investment expenditure is estimated at approximately 757.2 trillion VND, an increase of 287.2 trillion VND compared to the 2026 budget, focusing resources on implementing nationally important projects and tasks to promote economic growth. Simultaneously, 67.2 trillion VND will be allocated for other development investment expenditures to support investment, compensate for price increases at the Nghi Son Refinery project, and supplement charter capital for several enterprises and banks.
Recurrent expenditure in 2027 is estimated at approximately VND 980.9 trillion, an increase of VND 120.5 trillion compared to 2026. Priority will be given to implementing resolutions and conclusions of the Party, political tasks, national defense, security, social welfare, and salary reform. VND 30 trillion will be set aside as a reserve to ensure national financial security and safety. Recurrent expenditure will be allocated economically in accordance with Central Committee Conclusion 18.
According to Minister Ngo Van Tuan, the estimated local budget expenditure for 2027 is approximately 2.11 million billion VND, an increase of 476.6 trillion VND compared to the 2026 estimate, ensuring sufficient funding to implement policies and regulations according to decentralization and the tasks of managing and developing socio-economic activities at the local level.
The Minister of Finance emphasized that the state budget estimates closely adhere to the goals and tasks of socio-economic development and the national financial plan for the five years from 2026 to 2030. The projected state budget revenue and expenditure are at their highest levels ever, continuing the restructuring of the state budget.
The proportion of development investment expenditure reached approximately 43% of total expenditure, projected at 35.5% in 2026, creating an important resource for achieving double-digit economic growth targets. The proportion of recurrent expenditure remained at 50.6%, projected at 57.3% in 2026, while requiring rational allocation of recurrent expenditure, thorough savings, and ensuring the progress of the five-year national financial plan.
The remaining funds that need to be disbursed in the last months of the year are substantial.
Presenting the verification report on the aforementioned issues, the Chairman of the Economic and Finance Committee, Phan Van Mai, stated that total state budget revenue is estimated to exceed the projected figure by 20.8%, demonstrating the Government's close guidance in managing the state budget, and a more positive and sustainable shift in the structure of state budget revenue. However, central government revenue still accounts for less than 50% of total state budget revenue, showing no improvement compared to the 2021-2025 period.
The Chairman of the Economic and Financial Committee also clarified that 2026 will continue the budget stabilization period of 2021-2025, without recalculating the allocation of value-added tax and four other taxes including corporate income tax, personal income tax, special consumption tax, and environmental protection tax.
At the same time, it should be noted that the estimated revenue from land use fees for the whole year is expected to increase by about 35% compared to the budget, making a significant contribution to ensuring the expenditure tasks of localities. Therefore, with the real estate market showing signs of slowdown, it is suggested that the Government direct a thorough review of the estimated revenue collection to ensure it is in line with the actual situation.
You may also like
Regarding the 16.4% increase in total state budget expenditure compared to the projected figure, the Chairman of the Economic and Finance Committee stated that the Government has made efforts to ensure expenditure tasks are carried out according to the budget approved by the National Assembly. However, a significant amount of central budget funds remain unallocated and undisbursed, and he requested clarification of the reasons and solutions to address this issue. State budget expenditure for the first nine months reached 59.3% of the projected figure, and the estimated expenditure for the whole year will exceed it by 16.4%, indicating that a large amount of funds remain to be disbursed in the remaining months of the year.
The Chairman of the Economic and Financial Committee also proposed focusing on removing obstacles and accelerating the use of funds for science and technology, innovation, and digital transformation in accordance with Resolution No. 57-NQ/TW of the Politburo, and reviewing the needs for maintenance and repair of national highways to ensure resources are commensurate with the delegated tasks.
Regarding the 2027 state budget estimates, the Chairman of the Economic and Finance Committee proposed reviewing and calculating a realistic plan for the 2027 state budget revenue estimates, consistent with forecasts of economic development and ensuring resources for the implementation of state budget expenditure tasks.
On the other hand, the projected state budget expenditure and development investment expenditure have increased significantly compared to the 2026 budget, but a considerable amount of capital remains unallocated. This indicates a continued situation of capital waiting for projects, reflecting limitations in investment preparation that reduce the efficiency of resource utilization and prolong project implementation time.
The Chairman of the Economic and Financial Committee proposed that the Government direct ministries and localities to thoroughly economize on recurrent expenditures, strictly manage spending within the budget and the capacity for state revenue collection, ensuring efficiency and avoiding losses and waste.

articles.summary: Singapore’s economy grows more than 5.0pc amid AI boom  The Financial Express
articles.full_text:
Singapore’s economy grew more than 5 percent in the most recent quarter, continuing an AI-fuelled boom that has made the city-state one of the fastest-growing advanced economies.
Gross domestic product (GDP) grew 5.4 percent year-on-year between July and September, down from a 6.2 percent expansion in the second quarter, according to advance government estimates released on Wednesday.
Manufacturing, which is dominated by the city-state’s semiconductor industry, grew 7.5 percent, according to the estimates from the Ministry of Trade and Industry.
Increased output in “electronics, precision engineering, transport engineering and general manufacturing clusters” drove growth, the ministry said, offsetting declines in the chemicals and biomedical sectors.
Construction, including AI-related investments such as data centres, expanded 8.8 per cent, according to the figures.
Despite the heady expansion, Singapore’s central bank left its monetary policy settings untouched in its latest announcement on Wednesday, citing expectations that AI demand will cool in 2027.
The Monetary Authority of Singapore, which manages monetary policy through currency exchange rates rather than interest rates, said it expected core inflation to average 1.5–2.0 percent in 2026.
“Global AI-driven growth is expected to ease in the latter half of next year from its current exceptional pace, while higher interest rates, amid elevated inflation in the advanced economies, would weigh on final demand growth,” the central bank said in a statement.
Singapore is a major global player in the booming chip sector, a position that has helped it weather choppy economic conditions, including the energy shock prompted by the US-Israel war on Iran.
The Southeast Asian city-state accounts for roughly 10 percent of global semiconductor output and 20 percent of semiconductor equipment production, according to government figures.
Yeow Hwee Chua, an assistant professor of economics at Nanyang Technological University, described Singapore’s economic performance as “impressive for a high-income economy, especially given the uncertain global environment”.
“The global technology investment boom has been an important driver,” Chua told Al Jazeera.
“Strong demand for electronics has supported manufacturing and related wholesale trade, illustrating how Singapore benefits from its position in global supply chains,” he said.

TPO - Total customer deposits at credit institutions reached approximately VND 17.77 million billion at the end of August, an increase of nearly VND 1.26 million billion compared to the end of 2025. However, according to research, liquidity pressure still needs to be monitored as credit enters the peak season at the end of the year.
According to data released by the State Bank of Vietnam, by the end of August, total customer deposits at credit institutions reached approximately VND 17.77 million billion, an increase of over VND 310,000 billion compared to the previous month, equivalent to a 1.78% increase.
Overall, in the first eight months of the year, deposits from economic organizations and individuals increased by nearly 1.26 trillion VND compared to the end of 2025, equivalent to about 7.6%. Compared to the same period last year, the size of deposits increased by 11%, showing that the bank savings channel continues to attract a large amount of capital from the economy.
Notably, household deposits continued to be the main driver. At the end of August, the balance of household deposits reached approximately VND 11.43 million billion, an increase of nearly VND 214,000 billion compared to the end of July, equivalent to 1.91%. This is the highest level ever recorded.
Compared to the end of 2025, household deposits increased by nearly 1.1 trillion VND, equivalent to 10.63%. The proportion of household deposits in total deposits at credit institutions also increased from 62.58% at the end of last year to approximately 64.34%.
You may also like
Meanwhile, deposits from economic organizations reached approximately 6.34 million billion VND at the end of August, an increase of over 96,000 billion VND, equivalent to 1.54%, compared to the previous month. This development shows that capital flows from the household sector are making a significant contribution to the growth of deposits in the banking system.
With rising interest rates, deposits remain attractive.
One of the factors supporting the increase in deposits is the upward trend in savings interest rates since the end of last year, which continued to rise in the first few months of this year. Many banks continuously adjusted their interest rate schedules to attract capital, while some banks even offered higher preferential interest rates through direct agreements with customers.
For about a month now, many private banks have been offering customers deposit interest rates of up to 7-9% per year, applicable to amounts ranging from tens to hundreds of millions of VND. Some banks such as NCB, LPBank,SHB , HDBank, MSB, MB, MBV, and Vikki have been reported to be applying interest rates of 8.5-9.6% per year for some deposits with terms of 6-12 months. The actual rate depends on the product, applicable conditions, deposit amount, and the agreement between the customer and the bank.
In its 2027 Investment Strategy Outline Report, SSI Research's analysis team noted that deposits have recovered strongly after a period of almost no growth in the first quarter of 2026. In particular, from June to September, deposits increased by 10.6% compared to the beginning of the year, supported by accelerated disbursement of public investment, which helped bring funds from the budget back into the banking system.
In addition, rising savings interest rates, coupled with less attractive competing investment channels such as real estate, gold, foreign currency, and cryptocurrencies, have also contributed to the inflow of funds into banks.
You may also like
According to SSI Research, time deposits remain an attractive investment channel in 2027, considering risk adjustments, especially with gold prices fluctuating sharply, the real estate market slowing down, and cryptocurrencies lacking a detailed legal framework.
Analysts predict that the issuance of certificates of deposit and bonds could accelerate in 2027, becoming an additional tool for raising capital to narrow the gap between lending and deposit mobilization.
Despite improved fundraising, SSI Research believes that liquidity pressure still needs to be monitored, especially in this fourth quarter, when credit demand typically increases towards the end of the year.

According to experts, for the policy to be effective, in addition to reducing capital costs, it is necessary to facilitate sales, strengthen market confidence, and improve businesses' access to credit.
Lowering interest rates should go hand in hand with improved access to capital.
At a meeting on monetary policy management for the final months of the year on the afternoon of October 16th, Deputy Prime Minister Nguyen Van Thang requested the urgent, effective, and timely implementation of solutions to reduce lending interest rates by 1.5-2% for production, business activities, and priority sectors.

Priority sectors continued to record positive credit growth. Outstanding loans in the agriculture and rural sector accounted for approximately 22% of the total outstanding loans in the economy. Notably, the credit program for the agriculture, forestry, and fisheries sector, after being expanded to VND 185,000 billion, had disbursed nearly VND 238,120 billion cumulatively by the end of August, reaching 128.7% of the program's scale, with 88,434 customers accessing capital.

In addition, 19 commercial banks have implemented credit packages targeting economic growth and SMEs with a total scale of 407,000 billion VND, applying preferential interest rates at least 1% lower per year than the average rate for the same term.
Speaking with a reporter from Tien Phong newspaper, Associate Professor Dr. Dang Quang Vinh - an expert from the British University Vietnam (BUV) - said that the policy of reducing lending interest rates reflects a consistent direction in supporting the business community, removing difficulties for the economy, and promoting sustainable growth.
You may also like
In the context of a volatile global economy, the cost of capital and competitive pressure continue to be challenges for businesses. Therefore, reducing interest rates is crucial, helping businesses cut production and operating costs and creating conditions for credit capital to be used more effectively in the economy.
However, according to Mr. Vinh, for the goal of reducing interest rates by 1.5-2% to truly materialize, it is necessary to simultaneously consider the cost of capital for the banking system, the accessibility of credit for businesses, market demand, and future profit expectations.
Essentially, lending interest rates depend on the cost of funding, operating costs, and the level of credit risk. When the cost of funding increases, a sharp, widespread reduction in interest rates can put pressure on profit margins and the safety of the banking system.
Therefore, Mr. Vinh believes that interest rate reductions need to be implemented strategically, combined with flexible liquidity management, cost reduction at banks, and targeted interest rate support programs. Coordination between monetary and fiscal policies also plays a crucial role in creating room to reduce capital costs while ensuring the safety of the system.
Cheap capital is not enough.
Speaking with a reporter from Tien Phong newspaper, Professor Mac Quoc Anh, Director of the Institute of Economics and Business Development, said that to fundamentally solve the capital problem for small and medium-sized enterprises, it is necessary to shift from a mindset of simply providing credit support to building a financial ecosystem that suits the characteristics, scale, and development capacity of businesses.
Mr. Quoc Anh proposed the simultaneous implementation of seven groups of solutions, the first of which is to stabilize and gradually reduce borrowing costs according to market conditions. In addition, it is necessary to innovate credit assessment methods based on cash flow, economic contracts, electronic invoices, tax payment history, and payment creditworthiness. Businesses with stable orders and proven debt repayment ability should have access to capital, even if they lack real estate collateral.
You may also like
Another important solution is to improve the efficiency of credit guarantee funds by strengthening financial capacity, perfecting the risk-sharing mechanism between the fund, banks, and businesses, and simplifying procedures. In Hanoi , it is necessary to strengthen the connection between regulatory agencies, commercial banks, and business associations.
In addition, it is necessary to diversify credit products, develop factoring, order financing, supply chain credit, financial leasing, and accounts receivable-based financing.
Alongside boosting demand, it is necessary to improve supply capacity, enhance productivity, reduce logistics costs, and continue reforming the business environment. If demand increases but production capacity cannot keep up, the positive impact may be limited, and it may even create further inflationary pressure.
Professor Dang Quang Vinh argues that policy effectiveness should not be judged solely by the reduction in listed interest rates or the rate of credit growth. More important criteria include the number of businesses that actually benefit, the actual reduction in borrowing costs, the number of jobs created, and the added value achieved by the economy.
"The core issue is not just how to enable businesses to borrow capital at lower interest rates, but how to build enough confidence in the market for businesses to want to borrow capital and expand investment," Mr. Vinh emphasized.

The top five positions went to Princeton University in the United States, Paris-Saclay University in France, the University of Oxford in the United Kingdom, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in the U.S., and the University of Cambridge in the U.K.
Kyoto University was followed by Imperial College London in 17th place, Université Paris Cité in 18th, the University of Toronto in 19th and Columbia University in 20th.
The Hebrew University of Jerusalem in Israel ranked 24th, making it the next-highest institution in the ranking from Asia, followed by China's Tsinghua University in 26th place, right after Yale .
Seven other Chinese universities ranked between 32nd (Peking University) and 52nd positions, while the National University of Singapore followed at 56th.
China and Singapore have emerged as rising stars in Asian higher education, with their universities climbing global rankings in recent years.
The Program for International Student Assessment (PISA) 2025, conducted by the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD), ranked students in China the world's top performers in mathematics and science, as Singapore came second in both subjects.
The ShanghaiRanking focuses on mathematics research rather than overall university performance. ShanghaiRanking uses data from 2020 to 2024 and requires universities to have published at least 100 mathematics papers during that period to qualify.
Bibliometric data are drawn from Web of Science and InCites. Indicators include papers published in first-quartile (Q1) journals, category-normalized citation impact and internationally co-authored papers.
Category-normalized citation impact compares the citations received by a university's papers with the average for publications in the same subject, year and publication type.
As a result, the ranking emphasizes research strength and influence rather than undergraduate teaching quality, student experience, or graduate employment. Its results should therefore be interpreted as a measure of mathematics research performance, not a comprehensive assessment of mathematics degree programs.

articles.summary: Burial of Mahathir’s wife Hasmah brings into focus Malaysia’s forgotten national cemetery  The Straits TimesTun Mahathir’s health improves, but not ready to leave hospital  The VibesMarina Mahathir grateful for public's prayers, visit to late mother's grave  The StarMalaysia's former PM Mahathir returns to public eye in better spirits after wife Siti Hasmah's death  AsiaOne.com“She Was Ready To Leave Us All” Tun Siti Hasmah Passes At 100, Mahathir Says Goo...

AI generated
PUTRAJAYA – The grave of Siti Hasmah Mohamad Ali, wife of former Malaysian prime minister Mahathir Mohamad, has become a pilgrimage site for visitors and well-wishers from across the country, mourning the passing of the much-loved “mother of the nation”. She died on Sept 28.
Located at the southernmost end of Putrajaya, Malaysia’s administrative capital, the site has been surrounded by temporary hoardings, with canopies and chairs set up for the comfort of visitors, including Mahathir himself, who has been visiting almost daily.
Their daughter Marina Mahathir expressed her gratitude for the steady stream of visitors, saying the family was “truly grateful for their prayers and visits”.
“Every time I visit the grave, I see many people coming,” Marina said at a memorial service for Hasmah on Oct 13. “We are all deeply touched and thankful for their prayers.”
Hasmah, who died at the age of 100, had been expected by some to be buried at the Makam Pahlawan, or Heroes’ Mausoleum, at the National Mosque in Kuala Lumpur. Two of her predecessors, the wives of former prime ministers Abdul Razak Hussein and Hussein Onn, were buried there after their deaths in 2020 and 2014 respectively, near their husbands.
Grand vision, abandoned
So, when it was announced that she would be buried at Pusara Negara, or the National Cemetery, in Putrajaya, the reaction was a mix of confusion and curiosity.
Some wondered why she was not laid to rest at the Heroes’ Mausoleum. Others had a more basic question: What exactly is Pusara Negara?
The story of Pusara Negara reveals a grand national vision that was never realised. First proposed more than five decades ago as a tribute to Malaysians who had served their country, Pusara Negara was originally planned for Bukit Kiara, before the land was earmarked for a golf course.
The cemetery that eventually emerged in Putrajaya was a far more modest undertaking.
The original site was Bukit Kiara, then a hilly rubber plantation.
The 1982 Pusara Negara masterplan described it as “much different than the design for a traditional cemetery or graveyard”, envisioning “a cemetery within a park” that made full use of Bukit Kiara’s terrain.
The 89ha complex was to have a grand entrance, a ceremonial boulevard and a plaza where final tributes to national heroes would be made.
The cemeteries themselves were to occupy seven hills, with separate burial grounds for Muslims, Buddhists, Christians, Hindus and Sikhs, as well as land set aside for future expansion.
The planners envisioned enough space to bury the nation’s distinguished dead for more than 200 years.
The scale of that ambition becomes clearer when compared with the existing Heroes’ Mausoleum at Masjid Negara in Kuala Lumpur.
Inaugurated in 1965, it saw its first burial in 1973 with the death of deputy prime minister Ismail Abdul Rahman. Since then, five of the seven plots beneath its main pavilion, reserved for former prime ministers and deputy prime ministers, have been filled, while the open-air burial ground beside it has become increasingly crowded.
At the time, the proposed national cemetery attracted support in Parliament. Then Batu Pahat MP Abdul Jalal Abu Bakar suggested in Parliament that national heroes already buried elsewhere be reinterred there.
“The aim is to ensure that when visitors arrive, they can see those who have rendered distinguished service; we will inscribe the life stories of the deceased on each grave, whether they passed away long ago, such as during the Second World War, or were figures like Mat Kilau and others, so that they may serve as a lasting legacy for future generations,” he said in 1977.
But the grand plan was not to be. In 1988, the government decided to use the Bukit Kiara land for a different purpose: a golf course.
The land was sold to Solarvest in 1992 to be developed as the Kuala Lumpur Golf & Country Club, as part of a privatisation drive “for the benefit of the country with the arrival of foreign tourists into the country”.
Explaining the decision in Parliament in November 1992, deputy speaker Ong Tee Keat said Pusara Negara could still be built on a much smaller scale.
“The existence of this golf course does not mean that the national mausoleum can no longer be established,” Ong said.
A modest reality
The name Pusara Negara disappeared from public discourse for more than two decades, resurfacing in 2013 when work began on a dedicated burial ground for national figures within an existing cemetery complex in Putrajaya’s Presint 20.
Unlike the grand ceremonial plaza and hilltop burials envisioned in the original plan, the present-day Pusara Negara is modest, with Hasmah’s grave lying beside the main thoroughfare, just steps from the carpark.
The administration building bearing the cemetery’s name, meanwhile, remains empty and cordoned off with tape.
Yet, the modest setting makes the cemetery a more accessible and welcoming place for ordinary Malaysians.
S. Murali, who travelled from Kapar, Klang, about 60km or an hour by road, said it made it easier for Malaysians from all walks of life to visit the much-loved Hasmah.
“If it was in Masjid Negara, it feels a bit awkward for us non-Muslims to come and visit,” the 39-year-old electrician said during his visit on Oct 3. “Here, anyone can come.”
For others, where Hasmah was laid to rest mattered little.
“The love and appreciation is with her as a person,” said Maznah Idris, who lives in Gombak, Kuala Lumpur. The 68-year-old homemaker spent half an hour by the grave, reading the Quran and offering prayers for Hasmah.
“We will visit her regardless of where she is laid to rest.”

articles.title: Prime Minister: We need to shift from "made in Vietnam" to "created by Vietnam". - Vietnam.vn

articles.full_text:
The Prime Minister urged businesses to change their mindset, shifting from "made in Vietnam" to "created by Vietnam"; from competing on price to conquering the market through quality, technology, and reputation.
On October 16th, the Vietnam National Brand Council and the Ministry of Industry and Trade held the ceremony to announce the 10th time that products have achieved the Vietnam National Brand status in 2026.
This year, 499 products from 227 businesses achieved the Vietnam National Brand status, spanning various sectors such as processing and manufacturing; agriculture and food; pharmaceuticals and medical equipment; finance and banking; telecommunications and technology; logistics and services.
Shift from cost advantage to value advantage.
Speaking at the ceremony, Prime Minister Le Minh Hung affirmed that the National Brand title is not only an honor and source of pride, but also a commitment to consumers and a responsibility towards the image of the country. Each product bearing a Vietnamese brand must demonstrate quality, credibility, and a desire to reach the world .
By 2025, the honored businesses are expected to achieve revenues exceeding 2.5 trillion VND, contribute over 133 trillion VND to the state budget, and create stable jobs for more than 760,000 workers.
According to Brand Finance, Vietnam's national brand value is projected to reach over US$462 billion in 2026, a 45.14% increase compared to 2020, ranking 32nd out of 193 countries. The total value of Vietnam's top 100 brands is estimated at US$43 billion, an 11% increase from the previous year.
According to the Prime Minister, these figures not only reflect the breakthrough development of the economy but also show the growing confidence in Vietnamese products. Brands are not only assets of businesses but also create competitiveness, prestige, and national standing.
"Strong brands build strong businesses; strong businesses contribute to strengthening the self-reliance and self-sufficiency of the economy, making the country powerful and prosperous," the Prime Minister emphasized.
However, the Prime Minister also pointed out that many good products still lack strong brands, and their added value and ability to dominate the market remain limited.
Export revenue from businesses with products achieving National Brand status accounts for only about 11% of their total revenue, equivalent to 2.3% of the country's total export turnover. Meanwhile, investment in research, core technologies, intellectual property protection, and anti-counterfeiting measures has not yet met the requirements.
In this new phase of development, Vietnam is determined to achieve two strategic goals for the next 100 years, striving for an average GDP growth rate of 10% or more per year during the period 2026-2030.
The Party's strategic resolutions also open up new development opportunities. Specifically, Resolution 68 sets a target of having at least 20 large enterprises participating in global value chains by 2030; and for the private sector to grow by 10-12% annually, contributing approximately 55-58% of GDP.
Resolution 79 sets a target of having 50 state-owned enterprises in the top 500 in Southeast Asia and 1-3 enterprises in the top 500 in the world by 2030.
To realize these goals, the Prime Minister emphasized the need for a strong shift from cost advantage to value advantage; from processing and assembly to innovation and design; and from market participation to asserting a leading position.

Accordingly, businesses need to proactively improve productivity, increase domestic value, expand market share, and participate deeply in global value chains; considering brands as long-term strategic assets. Leading enterprises must lead the way, pave the way, and spread standards of quality, governance, and social responsibility.
At the same time, we need to make substantial investments in core competencies, science and technology, innovation, and digital transformation.
"Strengthen research and development, master technology, design, and invention; raise quality standards, green standards, and traceability. Apply data and artificial intelligence in brand management, focusing on customer experience. Shift from 'made in Vietnam' to 'created by Vietnam'; from competing on price to conquering through quality, technology, and reputation," the Prime Minister demanded.
The Prime Minister also urged businesses to develop distribution systems, partnerships, and after-sales services; protect intellectual property, maintain Vietnamese identity in each market, and effectively utilize free trade agreements (FTAs). Vietnamese brands not only need to be present but also need to have a sustainable position, be known, trusted, and chosen by the market.
Along with that, there is a shift from isolated development to collaboration, jointly upgrading Vietnam's value chain.
"Large enterprises lead the ecosystem, supporting small and medium-sized enterprises in improving technology, quality, and management. Healthy cooperation, resource sharing, and joint building of a solid industry and supply chain are essential. A strong national brand is impossible without strong enterprises and value chains," the Prime Minister said.
Businesses also need to persistently build a business culture of integrity, transparency, and responsibility; uphold the rule of law, protect workers and the environment; and avoid fraudulent origin claims and the sale of counterfeit goods.
"A brand can be built on quality and innovation, but it can only endure through credibility. Maintaining the reputation of a business is also maintaining the honor of the national brand," the Prime Minister emphasized.
14 businesses have maintained their title for 10 consecutive years.
Minister of Industry and Trade Le Manh Hung stated that the 227 enterprises recognized this year possess nearly 5,700 trademarks, inventions, utility models, and more than 2,400 international certificates and standards.
After 23 years of implementation, the number of businesses with products achieving National Brand status has increased more than sevenfold, from 30 businesses in 2008 to 227 businesses in 2026. Notably, 14 businesses have maintained the title through all 10 selection cycles, and 84 businesses have been recognized for 5 or more cycles.
A new feature of this year's selection process is the increased weighting of the innovation criterion from 18% to 30% of the total score. The evaluation focuses on research and development capacity, application of science and technology, digital transformation, green transformation, and intellectual property, in line with the direction of Resolution 57-NQ/TW of the Politburo.
According to Minister Le Manh Hung, in the coming period, the National Brand Program needs to shift strongly from "selection and recognition" to "creation and partnership," focusing on four key tasks.
First, finalize the Strategy for the Development of Vietnam's National Brand until 2035, with a vision to 2045, linking the national brand with industry, local, and enterprise brands.

Simultaneously, it supports businesses throughout the entire process of building, managing, valuing, protecting intellectual property assets, and handling trademark disputes abroad, all based on digital data.
In addition, brand building should be linked with trade, investment, and tourism promotion; and free trade agreements and the network of Vietnamese trade offices abroad should be utilized to expand markets.
In particular, we will continue to raise the selection criteria according to international standards, strengthen post-accreditation monitoring, and resolutely remove from the Program any cases that no longer meet the requirements.
Some of the brands that achieved the Vietnam National Brand status in 2026 include: CHIN-SU, MEATDeli, WinEco, WinCommerce, Masan High-Tech Materials, Vinamilk, VinFast, Vietcombank, VietinBank, BIDV, Vietnam Airlines, TH true MILK, CADIVI, Viglacera, Rang Dong, SUNHOUSE, Petrolvietnam Gas, Vitto…
Masan Consumer is one of the businesses with the most products achieving the Vietnam National Brand status in 2026, with 13 products receiving recognition.
Ms. Le Thi Nga, Deputy General Director in charge of Research and Development (R&D) at Masan Consumer Corporation, said that the company's products are available in 26 countries in Asia, North America, and Europe, demonstrating that Vietnamese goods can compete in the international market with their quality and unique identity.
According to Ms. Nga, the company focuses on innovation, combining research on consumer needs with the application of science, technology, and advanced techniques to improve product quality and meet the diverse demands of the market.
Meanwhile, a representative from VTHM Group, the owner of the Vitto tile brand, stated that this is the third consecutive time the brand has been recognized as a Vietnamese National Brand. This achievement is thanks to the company's focus on applying modern technology, improving designs, and diversifying its product range.

articles.summary: CNCTech Chairman Nguyen Van Hung was honored with the "Outstanding Vietnamese Entrepreneur - Saint Giong Cup" award in 2026.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
A title, a message
 Initiated by VCCI in 2006, the "Outstanding Vietnamese Entrepreneurs - Saint Giong Cup" program honors the long-term development standards of entrepreneurs, from leadership and management capabilities, innovation, and business efficiency to professional ethics, responsibility towards employees, the community, and society.
 In 2026, the Saint Giong Cup enters its 10th year of selection. This year, the program will choose 100 outstanding entrepreneurs from nearly 300 nominations submitted by 45 agencies, ministries, localities, and business associations nationwide. Over the previous nine years, the program has honored 860 entrepreneurs across the country. 
 The "Outstanding Vietnamese Entrepreneur - Saint Giong Cup" 2026 awards program
 This year's award originates from Resolution 41-NQ/TW dated October 10, 2023, of the Politburo on promoting the role of entrepreneurs in the new situation. This year, the awards ceremony takes place as the country is pursuing major development directions: breakthroughs in science, technology, innovation, and digital transformation ; shifting the export structure from extensive to intensive, significantly increasing the proportion of high-tech processed and manufactured industrial goods; enhancing national competitiveness and participating deeply in global value chains; selectively attracting FDI, promoting technology transfer, and developing endogenous capacity. 
 Permanent Deputy Prime Minister Pham Gia Tuc delivered a speech at the event.
 According to Mr. Ho Sy Hung, Chairman of VCCI, the selection process for the 2026 awards will not only be based on scale, revenue, or profit, but also on the business performance and leadership capacity of the enterprises over the past five years, starting from 2021; their ability to maintain competitiveness, overcome difficulties, and contribute to the country's development. The group of entrepreneurs selected for the 2026 awards are leading and managing businesses with total revenue in 2025 of approximately 1.34 trillion VND, pre-tax profit of nearly 248,000 billion VND, tax contributions of approximately 97,000 billion VND, and employment for approximately 273,000 workers. 
 Deputy Prime Minister Pham Gia Tuc and businesspeople at the event.
 Speaking at the event, Politburo member and Standing Deputy Prime Minister Pham Gia Tuc affirmed that the Government acknowledges the efforts and contributions of the business community to socio-economic development, job creation, budget contributions, improving people's lives, and enhancing Vietnam's position. The Standing Deputy Prime Minister emphasized that the Party and State always consider businesses as the core force of the economy; strong businesses lead to a strong economy, and thriving businesses lead to a prosperous nation.
 For those visions to become a reality, the economy needs entrepreneurs who are willing to invest long-term in technology, manufacturing, and supply chains.
 For Mr. Nguyen Van Hung, his story bears a unique mark: he represents a generation of engineers who dare to leave their comfort zone to start businesses in the most challenging fields – industry and technology – and are gradually bringing Vietnamese businesses into the global supply chain. 
 Deputy Prime Minister Pham Gia Tuc and VCCI President Ho Sy Hung presented the "Outstanding Vietnamese Entrepreneur - Saint Giong Cup" award for 2026 to Nguyen Van Hung, Chairman of CNCTech Group.
 Entrepreneurial spirit and the desire to master technology. 
 
 In 2008, CNCTech started as a small CAM office, with the aspiration to empower Vietnamese businesses to master precision manufacturing technology. With a background as a polytechnic engineer, Mr. Nguyen Van Hung infused a technical mindset – precision, discipline, and continuous improvement – into the company's management.
 From that starting point, CNCTech has gradually developed into an integrated industrial ecosystem comprising three pillars: manufacturing technology, industrial solutions, and logistics services. Currently, the CNC ecosystem exports industrial products to more than 35 countries, providing integrated manufacturing services for high-tech industries such as automation, semiconductors, aerospace, and automotive. Simultaneously, it develops green and smart industrial parks, clusters, and logistics centers, contributing to attracting high-quality FDI and developing Vietnam's supporting industries. Furthermore, CNC invests in the logistics sector to complete the competitive edge of its ecosystem. 
 Mr. Nguyen Van Hung - Chairman of the Board of Directors of CNCTech Group and one of the TOP 20 entrepreneurs honored in the highest category.
 CNCTech Group is also a public company, with its shares traded on the UPCoM stock exchange under the ticker symbol CLI, placing high demands on the business regarding information transparency, corporate governance, and efficient use of investment resources. 
 
 
 To date, CNCTech has put into operation more than 150 hectares of factory and warehouse space to serve production and logistics. 
 On May 6, 2026, over 91 million shares of CNCTech Group, with the stock code CLI, officially began trading on the UPCoM market. This marks a milestone in the company's development and sets higher standards for information transparency, corporate governance, and efficient use of investment resources.
 Promoting the role of entrepreneurs in the community.
 Besides his leadership role at CNCTech, Mr. Nguyen Van Hung actively participates in organizations representing the business community, promoting production linkages, investment cooperation, and the development of supporting industries.

articles.title: Crypto flows in Vietnam are shifting - Theinvestor
articles.summary: Crypto flows in Vietnam are shifting  Theinvestor
articles.full_text:
Cryptocurrencies in Vietnam are no longer just a matter of price speculation, with demand expanding towards value transfer and storage, posing new challenges for the domestic market.
The global crypto market has undergone a sharp correction, but on-chain activity has not declined by a comparable amount. According to the 2026 Global Crypto Adoption Index published by Chainalysis on September 23, market capitalization at one point fell by 50%, equivalent to $2.1 trillion, while the value of on-chain activity declined by just 1.6%, from $9.5 trillion to $9.4 trillion, over the two 12-month periods ending in June 2025 and June 2026.
The divergence suggests that crypto assets are being used for purposes beyond price speculation.
$122 billion market, stablecoins gain traction
In a regional report published on September 30, Chainalysis estimated that crypto asset activity in Vietnam reached $122.2 billion between July 1, 2025 and June 30, 2026, ranking fourth in Central and Southern Asia, Southeast Asia and Oceania, behind Singapore at $284.1 billion, Australia at $173.1 billion and India at $135 billion.
The significance lies not only in the market's size. Vietnam's Utility Index, which measures activity associated with practical use, rose 127% from the previous period, while its Financial Index, which tracks financial activity through platforms, fell 5%.
According to Chainalysis, the former reflects direct and cross-border asset transfers, while the latter captures financial activity conducted through platforms.
Notably, cross-border stablecoin activity in Vietnam reached about $10.5 billion, 1.5 times the domestic total of $6.9 billion. Stablecoins are crypto assets designed to maintain a stable value against a reference asset, typically the U.S. dollar.
Vietnam, Thailand and the Philippines recorded 5.4 million direct asset transfers worth less than $10,000, accounting for 14.4% of the global total. More than 80% of domestic transfers in this category were below $1,000, with an average value of $618.
Chainalysis quoted Nicole Nguyen, co-founder of APAC DAO, as saying that some Vietnamese users hold stablecoins as a store of value linked to the U.S. dollar. Freelancers and people working across borders are also driving direct transactions.
Nevertheless, Chainalysis estimated that $69.8 billion in assets flowed from Vietnam into centralized exchanges, indicating that emerging use cases have yet to fully displace investment and speculative activity.
Exchange race: from capital raising to platform testing
In Vietnam, businesses are preparing infrastructure for a pilot phase. The government's Resolution 05/2025/NQ-CP requires operators of crypto asset trading markets to have minimum paid-in charter capital of VND10 trillion ($386.58 million), along with requirements covering shareholders, technology and risk controls.
Among the prospective operators, Vietnam Prosperity Crypto Asset Exchange JSC (CAEX), part of the VPBank ecosystem, has taken concrete steps.
In April 2026, CAEX announced that OKX Ventures and HashKey Capital had signed investment and cooperation agreements with the company and its founding shareholders, VPBankS and LynkiD. The agreements aim to support technology development, security and liquidity.
At VPBank's 2026 annual general meeting, CEO Nguyen Duc Vinh said CAEX had fully contributed the required VND10 trillion ($386.58 million) in capital and completed an audit of its capital contributions, but had not yet received a licence to trade.
CAEX began testing its platform on September 6 and extended the program through September 25, restricting access to employees and selected partners. Its website continues to state that it is seeking a licence and has not officially opened trading.
Techcom Crypto Asset Exchange JSC (TCEX), which has capital contributions from Techcom Securities (TCBS), announced on May 5 that the Ministry of Finance had confirmed that certain groups of documents in its application were complete and valid, while requesting additional documents for the remaining sections. This did not constitute a licensing decision.
Among listed securities firms, VIX Securities has joined in establishing VIX Crypto Asset Exchange JSC (VIXEX), with initial charter capital of VND1 trillion ($38.66 million). VIX holds a 15% stake, FTG Vietnam owns 64.5% and 3C Company holds 20.5%.
VIX plans to use VND1 trillion from a share offering to make an additional capital contribution to VIXEX.
Sacom Crypto Asset Exchange JSC (SCEX), formerly known as LPEX, increased its charter capital from VND360 billion to VND5 trillion ($193.29 million) in August 2026, nearly 14-fold.
The company is also developing the SCEX Simulator platform as part of a digital asset education program, allowing users to trade with simulated funds rather than real money.
Outside the financial sector, Sun Group holds a 64% stake in Vietnam Digital Assets JSC, established in January 2026 with initial charter capital of VND1 trillion ($38.66 million).
Under Resolution 05, domestic investors who already own crypto assets may open accounts with organizations licensed by the Ministry of Finance to hold and trade those assets within the permitted scope. Six months after the first organization receives a licence, transactions conducted outside licensed systems may be subject to sanctions depending on the nature and severity of the violations.
However, the race to establish exchanges is only the first step. Another question is which assets can be issued and traded on these platforms.
In a recent article, Nguyen Huong Diu Ngan, an associate at the Tony Blair Institute for Global Change in Vietnam, proposed three potential areas for development: tokenizing trade finance, agricultural commodities and green infrastructure bonds.
One example is Argentina's Agrotoken model, which allows grain to be tokenized based on physical stocks verified in warehouses, helping producers gain access to credit.
The government's Resolution 05/2025/NQ-CP restricts the underlying assets and eligible participants in new issuance programs. As a result, domestic exchanges must not only attract investors but also develop product offerings that comply with the law, have clearly identified underlying assets, and establish the rights of holders.
As domestic crypto exchanges race to raise trillions of dong (VND1 trillion = $38.66 million) and complete their technology infrastructure, the challenge extends beyond securing licences. More importantly, they must find products that meet market demand within the legal framework, turning circulating crypto assets into organized business activity.
